title: Beta calibration for bounded signals: A two-stage likelihood framework for analytical chemistry
abstract: Calibration is central in analytical chemistry: given standards and instrument responses, the goal is to infer the concentration of an unknown. Departures from the Beer–Lambert law routinely induce nonlinearity and heteroscedasticity in spectrophotometric signals. We introduce a beta calibration model (BCM), a two-stage likelihood framework in which responses at both stages follow beta distributions and are linked to concentration via a smooth link (logit, probit, complementary log–log). BCM naturally handles bounded signals (proportions on (0,1) and, via rescaling, any (a,b)) and supports maximum-likelihood estimation, inverse prediction, and interval construction. In Monte Carlo experiments, BCM yields systematically smaller bias and RMSE and coverage closer to nominal than a range of alternatives, including linear and quadratic calibration, weighted least squares (WLS), a one-stage beta regression, a spline-based beta GAM, and a simple neural network, and is robust across links and designs. Applications to iron-in-water and tryptophan assays show that BCM provides more accurate and stable inverse predictions in challenging regimes where conventional approaches degrade. Modeling bounded responses with an appropriate beta likelihood materially improves calibration accuracy and uncertainty quantification in spectrophotometric assays.

title: CMFFS-LIBS: A comprehensive machine learning framework for magnesium quantification in alloys using LIBS with picosecond and nanosecond lasers
abstract: Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) enables rapid, in-situ analysis of aluminum-magnesium (Al–Mg) alloys within manufacturing processes. However, accurate quantification of magnesium (Mg) across a wide concentration range is challenged by complex spectral responses, such as self-absorption and plasma dynamics. This study investigates the effects of picosecond and nanosecond lasers on LIBS analysis of Mg in Al–Mg alloys and develops a machine learning framework to improve quantification under these two scenarios. Specifically, LIBS experiments were conducted using 355 nm ps and nanosecond lasers on samples with Mg concentrations of 0.62-10.32 wt%. Picosecond lasers resulted in stronger self-absorption and nonlinear spectral signals of some Mg lines, while nanosecond lasers provided more stable, linear responses. To mitigate prediction errors arising from the low intensity and fluctuation of linear Mg lines, this work develops the Comprehensive Machine Learning and Feature Fusion for Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (CMFFS-LIBS). This framework leverages the complementary information from high-intensity, nonlinear spectral lines to enhance prediction performance. It integrates data preprocessing (wavelet transform and Savitzky-Golay filtering), feature engineering (WBP, PCA, and XGBoost-RFE), and a Random Forest model. The proposed CMFFS-LIBS framework demonstrated good performance, achieving coefficient of determination (R2) scores of 0.939, 0.981, and 0.958 for the picosecond, nanosecond, and mixed datasets, with corresponding mean absolute errors (MAE) of 0.447, 0.166, and 0.318 wt%, respectively. This method provides a reliable strategy for online Mg quantification analysis in alloy production, achieving a data dimensionality reduction of over 94.8%, and can be extended to other elements.

title: Cardiotoxicity prediction of compounds based on multi-graph and multi-dimensional representations
abstract: Cardiotoxicity induced by compounds can range from minor electrocardiogram fluctuations to life-threatening arrhythmias. Computational approaches for predicting compound cardiotoxicity offer the advantages of lower cost and higher efficiency compared to experimental methods. We propose a novel method for compound representation that characterizes features related to toxicity using multi-graph and multi-dimensional features. We develop cardiotoxicity prediction models for nine categories of compounds (Arrhythmia, Cardiac Failure, Cardiotoxicity, Heart Block, Hypertension, Myocardial, hERG, CaV1.2, and NaV1.5) by employing graph neural networks and bidirectional gated recurrent units (BiGRU). Compared to previous studies, our model demonstrates superior or comparable predictive performance. Additionally, our model effectively captures toxicity alert structures in compounds and elucidates the structure-toxicity relationships. We develop an online server, CardiacTox (http://cardiactox.cqudfbp.net:88/), which is available for compound cardiotoxicity prediction and online retrieval of toxicity alert structures.

title: A UNetMam model for smart near-infrared spectroscopy analysis of fatty acid content in japonica rice
abstract: This study addresses the issues of redundant information and complex feature extraction in near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) data, and proposes a deep learning model named UNetMam, which integrates multi-scale feature extraction with global sequence modeling, to enhance the prediction accuracy of fatty acid (FA) content in japonica rice. The model architecture consists of a one-dimensional UNet (1D-UNet) module, a Mamba module, a global context module, and a regression head. The UnetMam architecture is trained by combining and tuning multiple parameters in different layers. The model was systematically evaluated on an NIRS dataset. The results show that UNetMam achieved the best performance on the test set, with a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.964 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.216, significantly outperforming comparative models such as PLS, 1D-UNet, Mamba, Transformer, and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN). To further elucidate the model's decision-making mechanism, the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method was introduced, identifying key spectral bands that contribute significantly to the predictions, thereby effectively mitigating the interpretability limitations commonly associated with deep learning models. This study not only validates the advancement and effectiveness of the UNetMam model in spectral regression tasks but also provides a novel deep learning solution characterized by both high accuracy and interpretability for quantitative NIRS analysis.

title: Physics-informed sequential data augmentation for three-phase flow modeling
abstract: Accurately describing oil-gas-water three-phase flow characteristics of multiphase pumps is desirable for the structure design and condition adjustment in crude oil extractions. Considering limited labeled data available and complex flow process features, a physics-informed sequential data augmentation method is proposed to generate enough samples for the modeling of three-phase flow processes. First, using the process knowledge from the multiphase transportation and quantified uncertainty from Monte Carlo dropout strategy, the complex regions of each condition are respectively identified and locally augmented samples. Then, all collected data and generated candidates are utilized as the original samples of the time variational autoencoder model for the global augmentation. Finally, a gated recurrent unit model is built to predict the flow rates of multiphase pumps. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method can capture the complex flow characteristics by introducing physics-informed augmented data.

title: Adaptive federated learning for slide-level biomarker prediction in breast cancer via misprediction risk analysis
abstract: Accurate and timely prediction of breast cancer biomarkers, particularly Estrogen Receptor (ER), Progesterone Receptor (PR), and Human Epidermal growth factor Receptor 2 (HER2), is critical for early diagnosis and personalized treatment. These biomarkers are typically identified from breast cancer biopsy samples, which are processed and stained via immunohistochemistry and then digitized using high-resolution microscopy to produce histopathological images, commonly used for AI-based prediction. Such images are complex, high-dimensional data that require advanced chemometric and machine learning techniques to extract clinically relevant information. While deep learning has demonstrated strong predictive capabilities, mispredictions remain common, largely because most studies rely on centralized learning with limited data confined to a single laboratory or hospital, raising concerns about patient privacy and data sharing. Federated learning offers a privacy-preserving alternative by enabling collaborative model development without exchanging raw data. Nevertheless, conventional federated approaches often struggle with mispredictions, particularly under heterogeneous laboratory conditions and multilabel biomarker classification tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel federated learning framework to tackle the challenge of frequent mispredictions in multilabel breast cancer biomarker classification. We introduce a secure decentralized misprediction risk analysis approach, allowing clients to share only anonymized risk features with the server and receive risk rankings in return, preserving privacy while enabling effective collaboration. Additionally, we present a risk-aware adaptive federated learning method that leverages these risk rankings to prioritize high-risk instances during model updates. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively mitigates misprediction risks and improves predictive performance in heterogeneous data settings, while maintaining strong privacy protection for breast cancer diagnosis. Our project code is available at: https://github.com/SheerazNWPU/FLRisk.

title: A statistical test and metric for matrix effects in non-linear calibration curves
abstract: Matrix effects in chemical analysis cause sample-dependent response changes that compromise quantification. Their systematic assessment is therefore an essential component of method validation. Currently, matrix effects are evaluated by comparing slopes between calibration curves, but this approach fails for non-linear response profiles common in modern methods. An L 2 norm-based statistical framework is presented that quantifies matrix effects through the integrated squared difference between calibration curves; a strategy not restricted to any specific calibration curve shape. The framework, which introduces a hypothesis test and generalized matrix-effect coefficient, is demonstrated for quadratic polynomial models, in which closed-form solutions are available, and four-parameter logistic models, necessitating numerical methods. For simple linear calibrations, both the proposed test and matrix-effect coefficient reduce to their classical counterparts, the slope t -test and slope ratio, thereby providing a unified framework for effect detection and magnitude. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate near-nominal Type I error rates and high power for detecting matrix effects under typical analytical conditions. Experimental validation using LC-MS showed increased sensitivity to matrix effects by identifying statistically significant response distortions undetected by conventional slope comparison, while UV protein quantification assays demonstrated specificity by correctly discriminating true matrix interference from baseline-related artifacts. An open-source R implementation provides an immediately applicable tool for validating non-linear calibrations in analytical method validation workflows.

title: Generative model-based two-dimensional correlated spectroscopy for oil film identification and thickness detection under temperature perturbations
abstract: Laser-induced fluorescence (LIF) technology in oil pollution monitoring is often constrained by environmental temperature fluctuations and spectral overlap. While two-dimensional correlation spectroscopy (2DCOS) can effectively enhance spectral resolution, its reliance on continuous variable-temperature experiments hinders its direct application in rapid in-situ detection. To address these challenges, this study proposes a feature enhancement method (CVAE-2DCOS) integrating conditional variational autoencoders (CVAE) with 2DCOS. This approach employs temperature as a perturbation variable, reconstructing real-time one-dimensional LIF spectra into multi-temperature virtual spectral sequences via CVAE, followed by two-dimensional feature expansion through 2DCOS. This significantly reduces dependence on continuous physical heating. Furthermore, this study compares the classification performance of Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA), Random Forest (RF), and Support Vector Machine Discriminant Analysis (SVM-DA) on one-dimensional spectral datasets. Support Vector Regression (SVR) and Partial Least Squares Regression (PLSR) are introduced to evaluate oil film thickness prediction capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that synchronous 2DCOS combined with MobileNetV3 outperforms other comparative models and methods in both tasks. It achieves an accuracy of 99.93% in oil film type identification and an R2 value of 0.997 in quantitative oil film thickness analysis. The proposed method circumvents the barriers of physical variable-temperature experiments, offering a novel approach for rapid in-situ oil spill monitoring.

title: Uncertainty calibration for latent-variable regression models
abstract: Uncertainty quantification is essential for scientific analysis, as it allows for the evaluation and interpretation of variability and reliability in complex systems and datasets. In their original form, multivariate statistical regression models (partial least-squares regression, PLS, principal component regression, PCR) along with their kernelized versions (kernel partial least-squares regression, K-PLS, kernel principal component regression, K-PCR), do not incorporate uncertainty quantification as part of their output. In this study, we propose a method inspired by conformal inference to estimate and calibrate the uncertainty of multivariate statistical models. The result of this method is a point prediction accompanied by prediction intervals that depend on the input data. We tested the proposed method on both traditional and kernelized versions of PLS and PCR. The method is demonstrated using synthetic data, as well as laboratory near-infrared (NIR) and airborne hyperspectral regression models for estimating functional plant traits. The model was able to successfully identify the uncertain regions in the simulated data and match the magnitude of the uncertainty. In real-case scenarios, the optimized model was not overconfident nor underconfident when estimating from test data: for example, for a 95% prediction interval, 95% of the true observations were inside the prediction interval.

title: Textile color grading using an improved Siamese network and hyperspectral technology
abstract: High-precision, non-contact color grading remains a challenging issue in textile quality control. In this study, a Siamese neural network based on hyperspectral imaging was developed for textile color grading. To address the high dimensionality of spectral data, the improved model combines convolutional feature extraction with a Manhattan distance metric to establish an effective similarity-learning framework capable of capturing subtle spectral differences between textile samples. Experimental results demonstrated that the improved method achieved strong classification performance, with an accuracy of 95.70 ± 2.48%, a precision of 96.28 ± 3.47%, a recall of 95.70 ± 2.48%, and an F1-score of 95.14 ± 3.19%. Compared with conventional chemometric models, the improved Siamese network delivered the best overall performance. The results further indicate that the Manhattan distance metric is effective for characterizing fine spectral differences in high-dimensional hyperspectral data. In addition, the predicted grading results showed high consistency with spectrophotometer measurements for representative samples, supporting the practical reliability of the improved approach. Overall, these findings demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of Siamese-network-based hyperspectral analysis for fabric color-difference grading and provide a new perspective for other material classification tasks in chemometrics.

title: Nonparametric CUSUM monitoring of paired-difference processes: A chemical engineering application
abstract: In many engineering and industrial systems, quality characteristics are inherently observed in paired form, such as pre- and post-treatment responses, input–output measurements, or readings from parallel and matched components operating under identical conditions. Proper monitoring of such paired observations is crucial, as ignoring the intrinsic dependence structure between paired measurements can substantially reduce statistical efficiency and impair the timely detection of process changes. The distribution of the difference of these paired quality characteristics is commonly unknown. To monitor such types of processes, parametric charting schemes are often inappropriate, and their in-control (IC) run-length properties are unstable when the distribution of the understudy process deviates from a normal environment. This study proposes two new nonparametric cumulative sum (CUSUM) charting designs for screening shifts in the location of the paired difference variables. The developed schemes are based on the sign and the Wilcoxon signed-rank statistics. The performance of the proposed designs is rigorously assessed using run-length (RL) profiles. The IC RL properties of the proposed designs are robust across different environments. Extensive comparative studies demonstrate that the developed charting schemes consistently outperform existing counterparts in detecting shifts in the median of paired difference variables. Practical applications related to chemical engineering, and a hypothetical application for robustness, are presented to demonstrate the proposed designs for effective monitoring in modern practical environments.

title: Addressing concept drift in wastewater treatment: a data-driven solution for predictive control and energy optimization
abstract: Artificial intelligence enables rapid wastewater quality monitoring through soft sensing techniques, effectively overcoming traditional digestion time limitations. This study evaluated four predictive models: support vector regression (SVR), polynomial ridge regression (PolyRidge), multilayer perceptron (MLP), and long short-term memory (LSTM). A dedicated dataset combining experimental measurements with ASM1-based simulations incorporating biological reactions and multiphase flow was established. Data preprocessing addressed concept drift from variability and outliers, while augmentation strategies enhanced the limited dataset. Optimized models achieved mean determination coefficients of 0.7867 (SVR), 0.7933 (PolyRidge), 0.52 (MLP), and 0.56 (LSTM). PolyRidge demonstrated superior accuracy with 6.37-min training, followed by SVR (10.74 min). Notably, MLP's aeration prediction accuracy improved exponentially with augmentation intensity (small noise injection, k-NN, and MICE R2 is 0.7346, 0.7583, and 0.7802), reaching 0.9845. Based on on-site tests and prediction analysis in Guizhou, after removing missing and abnormal data points, all models show good fitting accuracy for COD and TN, with SVR performing best overall. These findings highlight the potential of specific machine learning approaches for efficient and accurate wastewater quality prediction.

title: Integrating experimental data and machine learning for enhanced modeling of diclofenac release from calcium alginate–gum arabic microcapsules
abstract: This study focuses on the development and characterization of Sodium Alginate/Gum Arabic (Alg-GA) microcapsules for the sustained release of diclofenac sodium (DS). The microcapsules were prepared with varying concentrations of Sodium Alginate (Alg), Gum Arabic (GA), CaCl2, and DS, and characterized using Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FT-IR), X-Ray Diffraction (XRD), and SEM (Scanning Electron Microscopy) to confirm their chemical stability and morphological properties. Drug release profiles varied significantly depending on formulation parameters: higher alginate or Calcium Chloride (CaCl2) concentrations slowed release, while increased DS loading or agitation speed accelerated it. The high R2 values for Korsmeyer-Peppas (0.895-0.971) and Weibull (0.959-0.998) models revealed that the release of DS from Alg-GA microcapsules follows anomalous non-Fickian transport, with n ≥ 0.89 confirming Case II (swelling/erosion-controlled) release characteristic of spherical hydrophilic matrices, where water penetration triggers simultaneous diffusion and matrix relaxation. The MDT remained consistent (4–4.5 h), indicating uniform release. Encapsulation efficiency and swelling behavior were influenced by polymer ratios, with optimized formulations improving drug retention. Among several Machine Learning (ML) algorithms evaluated, the Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) regressor demonstrated superior performance in accurately predicting release profiles for unseen formulations (internal validation: R2 = 0.975, RMSE = 4.96% drug release in original units; prospective external validation on five new formulations: R2 = 0.968, RMSE = 5.38% drug release), demonstrating robust generalization with minimal performance degradation and accuracy within pharmaceutical acceptance criteria (±10% for dissolution testing). These findings highlight the potential of Alg/GA microcapsules for controlled drug delivery, with structural and morphological analyses providing key insights for formulation design.

title: Optimizing instrumental odour monitoring systems in drones by feature selection for odour detection and odour concentration estimation
abstract: Fugitive odour emissions from wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) present ongoing analytical and environmental challenges. Drone-mounted Instrumental Odour Monitoring Systems (IOMS) enable real-time, spatially resolved chemical sensing; however, large sensor arrays increase calibration complexity and cost. To address this, IOMS optimization is formulated as a machine-learning feature-selection problem. A two-stage selection strategy is introduced, combining Sequential Forward Selection (SFS) and Interval Partial Least Squares (iPLS) regression to identify minimal, information-rich sensor subsets and optimal temporal measurement windows. The approach is evaluated using data from a hexacopter-borne IOMS equipped with 21 sensors operating over an active WWTP. Sensors are ranked according to their incremental contribution to odour-concentration prediction error reduction, followed by refinement of measurement intervals to capture relevant temporal dynamics. Validation on independent flight data demonstrates that a configuration comprising only three sensors with optimized time windows retains or improves predictive performance relative to the full array. For quantification, the Bland–Altman limits of agreement improve from ±7 to ±5.3 dB od , and the Pearson correlation increases from 0.80 to 0.89. For odour-detection task, a single sensor achieves an AUC of 0.95, slightly outperforming the full sensor set (AUC = 0.93). Bootstrap analysis reveals variability in feature selection, though consistent trends are observed: ammonia sensors dominate quantitative models, whereas low-temperature MOX sensors are preferred in detection. The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of feature-selection strategies in simplifying IOMS hardware while preserving chemometric performance.

title: A novel adaptive multi-scale collaborative model for industrial soft sensing with scarce labeled data
abstract: In complex industrial processes, real-time monitoring of key quality variables is essential for improving product quality and ensuring safety, while labeled data are extremely scarce in practical scenarios due to measurement-related constraints. Existing semi-supervised soft sensing methods often fail to effectively mine inherent dynamic characteristics and temporal dependencies of industrial time-series data, leading to sharp performance degradation at low label rates, especially for offline modeling with historical industrial data. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel soft sensor model named Adaptive Multi-scale Collaborative Variational Autoencoder (AMC-VAE), which leverages a collaborative mechanism to capture the multi-scale dynamic characteristics of industrial time-series data. The core of AMC-VAE lies in a collaborative mechanism that integrates multi-scale decomposition, enhancement, and interaction to explicitly parse and strengthen the dynamic features inherent in industrial data. This mechanism enables hierarchical multi-scale feature extraction, capturing robust representations with limited supervision. Furthermore, within a semi-supervised framework, the model efficiently learns underlying data structures from abundant unlabeled data, significantly reducing reliance on supervisory signals while maintaining accuracy. Experimental results on two real industrial datasets demonstrate the superior prediction accuracy and generalization capability of the proposed AMC-VAE over existing mainstream semi-supervised methods.

title: Chemometric strategy for online tap water conductivity monitoring by electrical impedance in distribution systems
abstract: A chemometric-assisted strategy was developed for accurate, online tap water conductivity monitoring using electrical impedance spectroscopy in a low-cost Internet-of-Things device (NEMO). The study focused on optimizing instrumental settings and quantification models to achieve reliable conductivity measurements in the 15–750 μS/cm range, representative of real tap water conditions. Design of Experiments (DoE) was applied to evaluate the influence of key measurement parameters, while Principal Component Analysis (PCA) guided the selection of representative water samples, based on the chemical variability of tap waters in the Lombardia region (Italy). Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression was then used to model the full impedance spectra (2–150 kHz), achieving accurate conductivity predictions directly from raw data. The optimized model, built with data from 144 real water samples and validated on independent test sets, demonstrated excellent analytical performance (RMSECV = 35 μS/cm, RMSEP = 32 μS/cm) and high robustness under simulated distribution system conditions (30 L/h flow rate, 22 °C). Analytical figures of merit, including limit of detection (33–51 μS/cm) and quantification (98–154 μS/cm), were calculated following IUPAC-consistent chemometric procedures. This approach enables high-performance conductivity monitoring using compact and energy-efficient sensors, bridging the gap between device simplicity and analytical accuracy for online water quality monitoring systems.

title: Path-ComDim multi-block data analysis for the study of cachaça: Integrating sensory analysis with mass spectrometry
abstract: This study presents an integrated chemical–sensory characterization of cachaça using electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (ESI-MS) and multiblock chemometric analysis. Sixteen cachaça samples were analyzed in triplicate, including samples aged in wooden barrels from Minas Gerais, Brazil (Oak, Balsam, and Umburana), and flavored samples (spices, herbs, and fruits) from the Morretes region in the state of Paraná, Brazil. Molecular fingerprints were obtained by direct infusion ESI-MS operated in both positive and negative ionization modes, while descriptive sensory analysis evaluated appearance, aroma, and flavor attributes using a trained panel. The three datasets (ESI(+)-MS, ESI(−)-MS, and sensory) were integrated using the Path-ComDim multiblock method to identify common latent structures and correlations between chemical composition and sensory perception. The results indicated that high-mass ions, tentatively associated with lignin-, tannin-, and phenolic-derived compounds, are strongly related to wood-aged samples and to sensory attributes such as woody, vanilla, and alcoholic notes. Among the flavored cachaças, those containing cataia and banana showed greater chemical–sensory similarity to the aged samples. This approach demonstrates the potential of combining ESI-MS and multiblock chemometrics for the chemical characterization, differentiation, and quality assessment of cachaça and other distilled beverages.

title: A SHAP-guided ensemble learning framework for non-destructive aging evaluation of transformer insulating paper using near-infrared spectroscopy
abstract: Quantitative evaluation of insulating paper aging using near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy remains challenging. This limitation primarily arises from strong sample-wise matrix effects caused by overlapping absorption bands and physicochemical heterogeneity. These effects induce multiple spectral–degree of polymerization (DP) correlation patterns, which hinder the ability of a single regression model to adequately characterize the aging process. This phenomenon aligns with the Rashomon effect in chemometrics, where different models achieve comparable predictive performance while relying on distinct feature-attribution patterns. To address this issue, a SHAP-guided stacking ensemble framework is proposed for DP prediction. A spectral–DP database containing 473 samples from accelerated thermal aging experiments and field-decommissioned transformers is constructed. Spectral noise is reduced using Savitzky–Golay filtering, followed by wavelength selection via the MPA-CARS algorithm. Multiple machine learning models are employed to capture diverse spectral–DP relationships, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are utilized to identify complementary base learners. These models are subsequently integrated through stacking to enhance prediction robustness and generalization. On the test set, the proposed framework achieves an RMSE of 72.9 with a correlation coefficient of 0.91. Field validation on a 500 kV current transformer and several 10 kV distribution transformers provides preliminary evidence of generalization under real-world conditions. The results demonstrate that integrating complementary correlation patterns improves the reliability of spectral–DP prediction and provides a non-invasive and interpretable approach for in-situ aging assessment of insulating paper.

title: A knowledge-guided structured Bayesian regression framework for spectroscopic calibration
abstract: Motivated by the inherent structured sparsity of spectra, we propose a structured Bayesian regression (SBR) framework to enhance spectroscopic calibration. First, a variable importance hierarchical clustering (VIHC) strategy is introduced, in which regression coefficients (RCs) derived from partial least squares regression (PLSR) are hierarchically clustered to partition the spectrum into chemically meaningful intervals. Second, to leverage the synergistic effects among intervals, we develop a Bayesian adaptive interval-prior learning (BAPL) algorithm that enables global analysis of interval combinations. Specifically, each interval is initialized with an equal prior, and its prior is iteratively adjusted based on the marginal likelihood estimated for each interval. This global learning strategy systematically assigns larger prior weights to informative intervals while shrinking irrelevant ones toward zero, thereby capturing and exploiting structured sparsity. Experimental results on multiple real-world spectral datasets demonstrate that the proposed SBR framework not only improves prediction accuracy but also provides enhanced physicochemical interpretability and valuable chemical insights. More importantly, this work highlights the potential of structured Bayesian learning to bridge data-driven modeling and domain knowledge, offering a new framework for advanced spectroscopic calibration.

title: Validation in principal component regression: A case study of ash determination in wheat flour based on the CIELAB color space
abstract: Ash content is a key indicator of the wheat flour extraction rate and plays a crucial role in evaluating flour quality and classification. Traditional methods for determining flour ash are destructive, time-consuming, and require skilled personnel. In the present study, the CIELAB color space ( L*a*b* ) was used as a non-destructive method to estimate wheat flour ash content using multivariate principal component regression (PCR). The samples were provided from a milling unit, and all the analyses were conducted on-site at the industry. Model performance was evaluated by estimating parameters of merit, including accuracy (RMSEP = 0.0586, RMSEC = 0.0623, adjust, elliptical joint confidence regions), residual prediction deviation in calibration (RPDcal = 4.5094) and external validation (RPDval = 5.2113), inverse of analytical sensitivity (0.0131%), limits of detection (0.0431%), and limits of quantification (0.1306%). The findings demonstrated that combining the CIELAB color space with the PCR model can be used to accurately, rapidly, cost-effectively, and non-destructively estimate wheat flour ash content, making it a promising alternative to traditional quality control methods.

title: Continual learning-enabled probabilistic PLS for adaptive multimode quality-related process monitoring
abstract: Industrial processes are increasingly operating in multiple operating modes, where pre-trained process monitoring models fail to respond promptly when new operating modes emerge and cannot accurately distinguish between quality-related and quality-unrelated faults. To address this dynamic adaptation challenge, this article proposes a novel concurrent probabilistic partial least squares and modified Riemannian walk (CPPLS-MRWalk) for adaptive multimode quality-related process monitoring. Specifically, the continual learning strategy of Riemannian walk (RWalk) is employed to preserve information from previous modes and is embedded into probabilistic partial least squares (PPLS), enabling the model to monitor multiple operating modes. Meanwhile, a modified RWalk strategy is introduced, which incorporates task similarity to prevent performance degradation caused by excessive regularization. Furthermore, we derive the solution to the regularization-embedded PPLS framework, innovatively formulating the objective function to dynamically balance intra-mode feature extraction and inter-mode knowledge preservation across successive operating modes in industrial processes. In addition, a latent variable decomposition method tailored for PPLS is developed, enabling the model to distinguish between quality-related and quality-unrelated faults. The proposed method is validated through experiments on the Tennessee Eastman (TE) chemical process and a practical lean iron ore mineral processing process. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior quality-related process monitoring performance.

title: A study on Q and T2 in Partial Least Squares regression models
abstract: ABSTRACT A distinctive feature of Partial Least Squares (PLS) as a regression method is the definition of a region in the model predictor space, known as the PLSbox, such that the model should not be applied to objects outside this region. In multivariate regressions where the set of original variables is reduced to a smaller set of latent variables, typically in multivariate data generated by modern instrumentation in chemical analysis, this represents a notable advancement in identifying outlier data. Constructing the PLSbox requires assuming a probability distribution for the Q and T 2 statistics and computing a critical value for each at a desired confidence level. Despite its relevance, the impact of the chosen probability distribution has not been systematically examined. Parametric distributions like Snedecor’s F and chi-square have been widely accepted, even though their validity relies on the multivariate normality of the data, an assumption that cannot be made a priori . This work evaluates the effect of the usual parametric distributions for Q and T 2 on the PLS model in four different case studies, revealing a lack-of-fit issue in many cases, and what is more important, a notable impact on the PLS model structure. This problem disappears when a Gaussian kernel, which is distribution-free, is employed. Furthermore, the study highlights the impact of the interaction between the confidence levels chosen for Q and T 2 on the coefficient of determination of the accuracy line, suggesting that these levels should be chosen separately.

title: Polynomial model with Asymmetric Curvature Induced by Excess for mixture design: optimization of green anthocyanin extraction from Cenchrus purpureus using a standardless chromatographic response
abstract: Canonical Scheffé mixture models are widely used for binary systems, but their inherent assumption of symmetric component behavior restricts their ability to describe processes in which mixture components fulfill distinct physicochemical roles. This limitation is especially relevant for solvent-based extraction systems involving water and ethanol. In this study, the extraction of anthocyanins from leaves of Cenchrus purpureus . using water:ethanol mixtures were investigated, and an alternative modeling framework, named Asymmetric Curvature Induced by Excess (ACIE), was proposed to overcome this conceptual constraint. Experimental and simulated approach were evaluated in this work. Extractions were carried out by static maceration at room temperature using only water and ethanol, in accordance with Green Chemistry principles. The extracts were analyzed by HPLC-DAD, and a semi-quantitative approach was adopted in which the response variable was defined as the sum of the chromatographic peak areas of the two most reproducible anthocyanin signals. Canonical Scheffé linear and quadratic models were unable to adequately represent the system, exhibiting lack of fit and limited predictive capability. In contrast, ACIE, by incorporating asymmetric curvatures for modeling the excess of each component, achieved superior statistical performance and a more realistic representation of the response surface. The model predicted an optimal extraction region between 82 and 92% ethanol, consistent with the distinct roles of ethanol in promoting cell wall disruption and water in anthocyanin solubilization. These results show that ACIE effectively addresses a fundamental limitation of Scheffé-based models relative to asymmetries in binary mixtures and provides a flexible, chemically interpretable framework that may be applicable to other systems characterized by asymmetric component functionality.

title: MEMpre: Enhanced membrane protein type prediction via AlphaFold-driven protein large language models
abstract: Membrane proteins play critical roles in diverse cellular functions and are major targets in drug discovery. Accurate identification of membrane protein types is essential for high-throughput proteomic annotation but remains challenging due to the limited ability of existing computational methods to capture complex structural and sequential features. Here, we propose MEMpre, a novel Transformer-based framework that, for the first time, leverages AlphaFold-derived protein large language models (pLLMs) to achieve superior membrane protein type prediction. MEMpre employs a dual-stream architecture: one stream utilizes the pre-trained ProstT5 pLLM to extract AlphaFold-predicted 3D structural embeddings directly from sequences, while the other employs a residual Transformer block to model long-range sequence dependencies. This synergistic fusion enables MEMpre to effectively integrate critical structural context with deep sequence understanding. Extensive evaluations demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of MEMpre. On our curated dataset, it achieves an exceptional overall accuracy of 96.52%, exhibiting robust generalizability across diverse protein types, sequence lengths, and species. Crucially, on a widely adopted public benchmark, MEMpre sets a new high at 96.10% accuracy, significantly outperforming existing methods. SHAP analysis confirms the dominant contribution of pLLM-derived features, and ablation studies validate the necessity of our architectural design. MEMpre establishes a highly accurate, scalable, and structure-aware analytical framework, offering transformative potential for high-throughput proteomic annotation, structural biology studies, and accelerating membrane protein-targeted drug discovery.

title: Mixup deep features for augmented predictive data-driven modeling and quality analytics in chemical industrial processes
abstract: Due to the limitation of instrumentation technology, some quality-related variables are difficult to measure online in modern chemical industrial processes, which makes predictive modeling quite popular in recent years. With the aids of fast developed AI technology and data engineering, software-based quality prediction and analytics become more and more promising. However, due to the limited number of labeled training data samples, the performance of the quality prediction model is strongly restricted, especially for those emerging deep learning methods which typically require a large number of training data. In this paper, the mixup technique is introduced for augmentation of features provided by the lightweight deep latent variable model. After the deep latent feature space has been expanded by the mixup augmentation, predictive modeling can be carried out between the augmented features and the quality variables. Two industrial examples are provided for performance evaluation, based on which the superiority of the mixup feature augmentation method has been confirmed. Compared to the data augmentation made in the original variable space, the one implemented in the deep feature space is more effective for predictive modeling and quality analytics.

title: Machine learning decodes odor–intensity relationships in coatings: Bridging VOC chemistry to human perception
abstract: This study demonstrates the successful application of machine learning (ML) to decode the complex relationships between volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and human odor perception in acrylic binders. By solid phase micro-extraction (SPME) GC-MS analysis, thirty-eight volatiles were identified from sixty-seven binders. Various supervised learning models were evaluated to correlate volatile data with human sensory results. Among these models, the Random Forest (RF) model appeared as the most suitable model for this application. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identified nine key volatiles as primary sensory drivers. The feature selection process effectively improved Mean Absolute Error (MAE) values of the RF model from 0.64 to 0.52. This work advances the rational design of low-odor binders and sets up ML as a powerful tool to bridge VOC data to human odor perception in industrial applications.

title: Detection of vegetable-based fat adulterants in butter using portable near-infrared spectroscopy and semi-quantitative classification models
abstract: Butter adulteration, particularly with vegetable fats, is an age-old practice that has become increasingly sophisticated. This study developed and validated classification chemometric models using portable near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) and focusing on soft independent modeling of class analogy (SIMCA) to detect adulterants in butter. The results of this model were compared with partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) and one-class partial least squares (OCPLS). Seven adulterants were studied in a range between 2% and 100%: palm fat, margarine, and cottonseed, canola, sunflower, corn, and soybean oils. A total of 412 samples were analyzed, including 12 adulterated samples seized in an operation of the Brazilian Federal Police. A robust one-class SIMCA model performed an almost perfect classification, with their spectral interpretation indicating key variables associated mainly with C–H (fat) bonds. This interpretation was corroborated by an exploratory principal component analysis (PCA) model. Samples seized by the Brazilian police were effectively detected as non-authentic. The estimate of quantitative parameters, decision limit (CCα) and detection capability (CCβ), for qualitative methods allowed to establish semi-quantitative models. This approach provides a practical, non-destructive, and environmentally friendly solution for food authentication, addressing the urgent need for reliable methods in combating butter adulteration.

title: DeepSTAT3: An attention-enhanced 3D convolutional neural network with SPLIF features for STAT3 inhibitor discovery
abstract: Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription 3 (STAT3) is a transcription factor whose persistent activation drives oncogenesis and immune evasion, making it a high-value yet pharmacologically challenging therapeutic target. Conventional structure-based virtual screening (SBVS) methods often fail to capture the non-linear and spatially complex interactions of STAT3-ligand binding. Here we present DeepSTAT3, a deep learning framework that integrates three-dimensional convolutional neural networks (3D CNNs) with multi-head attention mechanisms and Structural Protein-Ligand Interaction Fingerprints (SPLIF). The model encodes protein-ligand complexes as 3D grids (24 Å3) with SPLIF-derived interaction features, enabling hierarchical learning of spatial binding patterns. Multi-head attention layers placed after the first convolutional block refine these features by focusing on pharmacophorically critical regions. To address class imbalance (active:decoy ratio of 1:50), we employed class-weighted loss functions during training. Using a scaffold-based split (80% training, 20% testing) to ensure chemotype diversity, DeepSTAT3 was evaluated on a standard test set and two progressively harder test sets with Tanimoto similarity <0.8 and < 0.75 to training compounds. On the standard test set, the model achieved PR-AUC of 0.76 (95% CI: 0.72-0.80), ROC-AUC of 0.76, and F1-score of 0.18, reflecting the expected precision-recall trade-off in highly imbalanced screening scenarios. On the hard test sets, DeepSTAT3 maintained robust performance with PR-AUC of 0.94-1.00 and ROC-AUC of 0.98-1.00, demonstrating strong generalization to novel chemical scaffolds. Comparison with baseline methods (SMINA, RF-ScoreVS, CNN-Score, SCORCH) showed DeepSTAT3 significantly outperformed all approaches (DeLong's test p < 0.01). Ablation studies confirmed that both SPLIF features and attention mechanisms contribute critically to model performance. DeepSTAT3 provides an accurate, interpretable, and target-specific scoring function for STAT3 inhibitor discovery, with a framework readily extensible to other therapeutic targets. The model implementation is freely available at https://github.com/sawera1312-ai/Stat3-Code-implementation.git.

title: Engineering an interpretable chemometric pipeline for sugarcane wine fermentation using synthetic spectra and explainable ensembles
abstract: Background Real-time spectroscopic monitoring of sugarcane wine is becoming increasingly important for quality and safety control. However, it remains less studied than established fermentations such as beer or grape wine, especially from a chemometric perspective. Objective To develop a mechanistically grounded synthetic spectral generation framework that enables interpretable machine learning for fermentation monitoring without extensive experimental calibration datasets. Methods We integrated kinetic fermentation modelling based on extended Monod-inhibition equations with realistic spectral simulation incorporating multi-scale noise artefacts. Nine machine learning architectures (PLS, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, DNN, CNN, LSTM, ResNet, Transformer, and Stacked Ensemble) were evaluated using SHAP-based explainability analysis and Bayesian bootstrap uncertainty quantification. Results Tree-based models achieved exceptional performance on purely synthetic validation data (R2 up to 0.997, RMSE ≈ 1.1 g/L), but all architectures collapsed when evaluated under simulated real-world conditions that introduced unmodelled matrix variability and instrument artefacts (R2 from −0.01 to −1.88). The simplest PLS model degraded the least but still failed to reach acceptable predictive accuracy, indicating a fundamental gap between the synthetic training distribution and realistic deployment scenarios. Significance These results show that even careful mechanistic, noise-aware synthetic spectra cannot guarantee successful domain transfer by themselves. Synthetic data remain valuable for model prototyping, architecture screening, and interpretability analysis, but must be complemented by targeted experimental calibration and synthetic-to-real adaptation strategies. Exploiting this limitation is critical for chemometric practice, as it reframes synthetic pipelines from “replacements” to “augmentation tools” for real fermentation monitoring.

title: A fault likelihood-based local-global fusion framework for nonstationary process monitoring
abstract: Affected by factors such as load fluctuations and external disturbances, modern industrial processes often exhibit significant nonstationary characteristics, which may conceal fault features and mask local incipient anomalies. To address these issues, this paper proposes a local-global fusion monitoring method based on fault likelihood weighting. First, a refined grouping strategy is implemented on high-dimensional monitoring data to ensure that variables within each group share strong correlations and similar dynamic evolutionary characteristics. Second, overcoming the limitation of traditional methods that directly discard nonstationary components, potential validity information is simultaneously extracted from both stationary and nonstationary subspaces to maximize the preservation of fault features. On this basis, local monitoring models are constructed for each subgroup to achieve precise localization of faulty groups and key features. Finally, a global monitoring model is established by fusing local statistics via a fault likelihood weighting mechanism, thereby realizing a comprehensive assessment of the overall operating status of the industrial process. Numerical simulations and experiments on the Tennessee-Eastman Process (TEP) demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.

title: Curriculum transfer learning of intermediate quality indicators in wastewater treatment plants using progressive neural networks
abstract: Although successful implementations of soft sensors to industrial wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) have been extensively reported, there are still spaces for technical improvements. Deploying multiple soft sensors for predicting water qualities at different intermediate sections of WWTPs can effectively improve the effluent quality control. However, it has been widely pointed out that the problem of insufficient process information arising from the fixed placements of hard devices may limit the performances of supervised modeling. Therefore, an innovative curriculum transfer learning (CTL) approach based on progressive neural network (PNN) was proposed and applied to data-driven modeling of spatially related chemical and biological oxygen demands in WWTPs. Based on information theory, the learning curriculums of spatially related quality variables were determined in the orders of increasing conditional entropy given the process variables. Through progressive model expansion and layer-wise extraction of abstract quality-inferring mechanisms embedded in well-trained soft sensors for effluent qualities, effective intra-plant knowledge transfer was achieved. In addition, models expanded from neighboring quality variables demonstrate better transfer performance than those derived from non-neighboring ones. By comparing the proposed models with their conventional counterparts, 42–60% of prediction errors were eliminated. Furthermore, through a series of interaction information analyses, it was explicitly revealed that synergistic contributions from different PNN blocks accounted for 11.1–96.3% of the predictive information, quantitatively justifying the ability of CTL approach to effectively migrate useful nonlinear quality-inferring knowledge to newer tasks.

title: A three-layer explainable stacking ensemble for monitoring subtle anomalies in chemical processes
abstract: The Industry 4.0 paradigm demands optimal performance in productivity, resource efficiency, and product quality. However, these objectives are often compromised by subtle, undetected anomalies, such as incipient faults or malicious attacks, and a lack of clarity among operators regarding the root-cause variables involved. To address this challenge, this study presents a novel explainable kernel-stacked ensemble designed to detect small-magnitude anomalies that are often hidden within the typical variations of industrial processes. The proposed monitoring scheme features a highly scalable three-layer architecture: (i) an embedded kernel preprocessing layer that simplifies high-dimensional data to uncover hidden correlations and enhance feature representation diversity, (ii) a prediction layer that fuses base learner outputs via a meta-classifier, and (iii) a Post-Hoc XAI layer that provides visual insights and quantifies the contribution of process variables during both detection and isolation stages. The effectiveness of the proposed method is evaluated using the Tennessee Eastman (TE) process, which emulates a realistic chemical plant with strong nonlinear dynamics and complex fault scenarios. The results demonstrate that the stacked framework outperforms individual base predictors in monitoring tasks. Furthermore, comparative analyses with recently published algorithms confirm the outstanding detection and isolation capabilities of the proposed method.

title: Determination and visualization of the distribution of water activity and moisture properties of roasted and ground coffees by near-infrared hyperspectral imaging
abstract: Moisture content and water activity are critical parameters routinely assessed in the food industry to evaluate physicochemical stability and microbiological spoilage. Coffee is no exception, as these factors strongly influence its quality and shelf life. In this study, near-infrared hyperspectral imaging (NIR-HSI) is proposed as a fast, simple, non-destructive, and safe alternative not only for determining these parameters, but also for spatially mapping their distribution within samples. Chemometric models were calibrated using average spectra to predict water activity and moisture content. The models achieved coefficients of determination (R2) of 0.87 and 0.88 for the prediction sets, with root mean square errors of prediction (RMSEP) of 0.03 and 0.23, respectively. However, pixel-level predictions in hyperspectral imaging are often limited by high noise and poor reliability. To address this challenge, the effect of macropixel size on prediction performance and spatial resolution was investigated. A macropixel size of 20 pixels (3.12 mm) provided stable predictions while preserving adequate spatial resolution. Overall, this study introduces a novel framework based on macropixel optimization to overcome pixel-level limitations, enabling robust and spatially resolved prediction of moisture content and water activity in heterogeneous coffee samples.

title: Enhancing anti-inflammatory small molecules prediction using transformer embeddings and hybrid features integration with ensemble models
abstract: Inflammation is a complex biological response that helps the body defend itself against toxins, pathogens, and injuries. However, prolonged inflammation can lead to chronic disorders such as cardiovascular diseases and neurodegenerative conditions etc. Developing effective anti-inflammatory small molecule drugs is essential for the management of all these conditions, but traditional methods are time-consuming and resource intensive. To accelerate this process, machine learning and deep learning approaches are widely used to predict the potential anti-inflammatory molecules based on molecular features. In this study, we used eight types of molecular representations, including fingerprints and descriptors such as Morgan, MACCS, and RDKit, as well as hybrid features like Morgan_RDKit, Morgan_MACCS, and MACCS_RDKit. Additionally, we incorporated transformer-based embeddings generated by Llama 2 and ChemBERTa. In total, 24 models were developed with Stacking Classifier on the hybrid features (MACCS_RDKit), achieving the highest performance, with an accuracy of 0.95, Mathews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 0.89, and sensitivity of 0.95 on an independent test dataset. These results highlight the effectiveness of hybrid feature representations combined with ensemble learning in enhancing predictive performance for anti-inflammatory small molecules. Moreover, SHAP analysis revealed consistent key descriptors and structural fragments that significantly impact the model's predictions.

title: Classifying graft survival using a new filter statistical feature selection method
abstract: Classifying kidney graft status is important due to the difficulties in locating organs for kidney transplantation. Even with improvements in acute rejection results, accurate prediction of graft status remains difficult. Machine learning tools provide more options to classify kidney transplant patients. Choosing appropriate variables determines the efficiency of any prediction approach. The selection procedure of the important variable is a significant preprocessing step which can choose the fewest relevant variables from the attributes. This paper introduces a new novel variable selection technique that mixes two statistical methods with filter method to classify kidney transplant status after kidney transplantation. It combines the univariate analysis method and information gain method with the multivariable analysis method. The selected attributes are classified using support vector machine, decision tree, and naïve Bayes with and without using the proposed method. Also, it was evaluated with the state of the art algorithms. The outcomes reveal that results is better in terms of classification metrics with the proposed method. The decision tree with attribute selection technique is the best accuracy, precision, and f-measure. The Naïve Bayes with attribute selection technique is the best recall.

title: Non-destructive assessment of maturity stage and comprehensive maturity characterization factors in Xanthoceras sorbifolia bunge using visible/near-infrared hyperspectral imaging
abstract: Maturity critically impacts rational harvesting of Xanthoceras sorbifolia Bunge, influencing yield, oil quality, and postharvest handling. This study pioneered visible/near-infrared hyperspectral imaging (HSI) for non-destructive maturity assessment of Xanthoceras sorbifolia Bunge using a proposed maturity characterization factor (MCF) generated from nine key indicators. All 628 hyperspectral images across four maturity stages of Xanthoceras sorbifolia Bunge were collected, and 19 maturity-related physicochemical parameters were measured. Band variability was analyzed using principal component analysis (PCA), and maturity discrimination models were developed by partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), genetic algorithm-support vector machine (GA-SVM), residual network (ResNet), and convolutional neural network-Transformer (CNN-Transformer), incorporating spectral preprocessing. For simplified models, feature wavelengths were extracted using principal component (PC) loading, successive projection algorithm (SPA), and stability competitive adaptive reweighted sampling (sCARS). Developed partial least squares regression (PLSR) showed that model based on second-order derivative spectra, SPA, and PLS-DA (FD2-SPA-PLS-DA) performed well (Accuracy = 98.73%, Kappa = 0.9830). Performance was then significantly improved by combining spectral, color, and texture features (Accuracy = 99.36%, Kappa = 0.9915). For MCF prediction, model based on first-order derivative spectra, SPA, and PLSR (FD1-SPA-PLSR) yielded the optimal results with R2 P = 0.7534, root mean square error of prediction (RMSEP) = 0.1853, and relative percent deviation (RPD) = 2.0138. Finally, an MCF distribution map generated using the preferred simplified model successfully visualized maturity heterogeneity in Xanthoceras sorbifolia Bunge. Our work demonstrates the first application of HSI for rapid, non-destructive Xanthoceras sorbifolia Bunge maturity assessment, establishing it as an effective tool for further field application.
