title: Elemental Blend Solver: An open-source browser tool for polymer blend identification by non-negative least squares
abstract: The Elemental Blend Solver (EBS v9.0.2) is a browser-native application for reconstructing the elemental composition of a target compound from a massweighted blend of up to five source materials. EBS formulates the problem as constrained Non-Negative Least Squares (NNLS) and applies the Lawson–Hanson active-set algorithm to produce non-negative mixing fractions summing to unity. The software embeds a curated 73-material database spanning 20 elements in a single HTML file (∼255 KB) requiring no installation, server, or network access. Sixteen analysis tools comprise seven chart views (six quantitative plus one pedagogic Convergence Plot) and nine quantitative panel diagnostics, including Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis, PCA database coverage mapping, ternary SSR contouring, exhaustive optimal blend search, and solution space exploration. A dimensionless fit index bounded (0, 1], the Global Decomposability Score (GDS), provides an instrument-independent blend-quality signal requiring no statistical tables. Validation across a 20-molecule test suite confirms exact recovery (SSR < 10−8 ) for hull-interior targets and minimum-error approximation for infeasible targets. Computational validation against published CHNS combustion data [32] confirms noise-floor elemental recovery (RMSEpp ≤ 0.050 pp, within single-σ CHN instrument noise) across seven fully-represented blend cases (p ≥ 0.860); absent-source cases are correctly identified by the χ 2 diagnostic (p < 0.001), confirming graceful degradation. Halogen mass balance constrains PVC identification to sub-0.1 pp precision. Together, these capabilities deliver a complete, validated analytical workbench accessible to any practitioner via a standard web browser. EBS is freely available under the MIT license (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19263118).

title: An interpretable knowledge-enhanced soft sensor framework for basic oxygen furnace endpoint prediction via LLM-driven feature engineering and SHAP-based threshold analysis
abstract: Basic oxygen furnace (BOF) steelmaking is a high-temperature chemical reaction process where endpoint carbon content and temperature are critical variables determining molten steel quality. Traditional data-driven models rely on manual feature engineering and iterative hyperparameter tuning, with predictions difficult to translate into actionable guidelines. This paper proposes an interpretable soft sensor framework integrating large language model (LLM)-based knowledge feature engineering, Tabular Prior-data Fitted Networks (TabPFN), and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based threshold analysis. The framework generates physicochemical knowledge-enhanced features via multiple LLMs, combines correlation screening with recursive feature elimination with cross-validation (RFECV) to select the optimal feature subset, applies TabPFN for rapid endpoint prediction, and extracts sensitive intervals and operational thresholds via SHAP dependence fitting. Using 814 heats from a 220-ton BOF, the model achieved test-set coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.5318 and 0.8315, hit rates (HR) of 79.75% (±0.01%) and 92.64% (±10 °C), and training times of 0.3805 s and 0.3944 s for carbon content and temperature, respectively. Against state-of-the-art models, R2 increased by 5.75% and 1.66%, HR by 3.06 and 1.23 percentage points, and training speeds by factors of 402 and 453, respectively. SHAP analysis identified a high-sensitivity interval of [1682, 1792] kg for light-fired dolomite on carbon content, and an efficient temperature regulation region within 700 kg of ore consumption. Over 52 industrial heats, HR reached 94.23% and 100% for carbon content and temperature. These results demonstrate that the framework enables rapid BOF endpoint prediction and operational threshold extraction, providing a quantitative basis for endpoint control.

title: Hybrid kernel deep orthogonal subspace analysis-based anomaly detection for key performance indicators
abstract: In modern industrial processes, the accurate detection of key performance indicators (KPIs) is often challenged by high system nonlinearity compounded by incipient anomaly characteristics. To address this issue, a hybrid kernel deep orthogonal subspace analysis algorithm is proposed in this paper. First, a hybrid kernel combining Gaussian and polynomial kernels is utilized to project the original nonlinear process data onto a high-dimensional feature space. This projection enhances linear separability, while the Gaussian component preserves local neighborhood similarities and the polynomial component captures global high-order feature interactions. Within this feature space, a kernel correlation matrix (KCM) is constructed to characterize the associative properties of the relevant information between process inputs and KPIs. A deep singular value decomposition scheme is then applied to this KCM to hierarchically decompose the KPI-related information into multiple kernel subspaces. Hierarchical decomposition further enables the construction of a multi-order subspace structure, which significantly enhances sensitivity to incipient anomalies that are easily obscured by noise in first-order projections. Furthermore, complexity is assessed via floating-point operations, serving to illustrate the feasibility for both the training and detection phases. Finally, experiments on the penicillin fermentation process and thermal power plant process are carried out. The practical applicability of the proposed method is verified, and superior performance over state-of-the-art techniques is demonstrated.

title: Scale analysis method coupled with a salp swarm algorithm to study the heat transfer rate of liquid metal nanofluids
abstract: Background The problem of natural convection heat transfer of nanofluids subjected to an external magnetic field has been extensively studied in recent years because of its various applications in different fields of engineering. Most of these studies have focused on conventional nanofluids obtained by dispersing nanoparticles in ordinary liquids such as water, however, few studies have focused on liquid metal nanofluids. Compared to traditional base fluids, liquid metals exhibit a much higher thermal and electrical conductivities, which significantly alters the effect of adding nanoparticles on the heat transfer rate. Novelty and methodology In this paper, we propose to study the heat transfer rate of molten gallium with suspended nanoparticles in a cubic cavity laterally heated and subjected to an external magnetic field. First, for pure molten gallium, the scale analysis method is used to obtain a general correlation of the heat transfer rate which depends on several adjustable parameters. Then, based on the already published experimental data, the salp swarm algorithm is used to identify these parameters. The obtained correlation is then developed for nanofluids whose base fluid is molten gallium. The effect of the addition of Cu or Al2O3 nanoparticles on the heat transfer rate is studied. Significant results For pure molten gallium, the results show that the maximum error between the predicted and experimental data is less than 3%, which demonstrates that the scale analysis method coupled with an optimization algorithm represents a promising approach to obtain precise correlations. For nanofluids, the results show that the improvement of the heat transfer rate by the addition of Cu nanoparticles is generally better than that of Al2O3, but it strongly depends on Hartmann and Rayleigh numbers. Also, for weak Hartmann numbers, Al2O3 nanoparticles are useless because the heat transfer rate decreases.

title: CLKAN-DBPred: Leveraging pre-trained protein language models with convolutional layer Kolmogorov-Arnold Network for predicting DNA-binding proteins
abstract: DNA-binding protein prediction helps to understand the fundamental process of life activities. Existing computational methods targeting large-scale DBPs are cost-effective and fast compared to conventional biochemical experiments. However, many earlier in-silico techniques rely on shallow or handcrafted descriptors that may not fully capture contextual sequence information. Recent pre-trained biological language models (BLMs) improve sequence representation by learning rich contextual characteristics from proteins. Methods In this study, we develop CLKAN-DBPred, an integrated framework for predicting binding activity of DBPs using a fine-tuned approach that integrates DistilProtBert, Prot-T5, and ESM2 embeddings, the RFE-F7-1195 representation, and a convolutional KAN classifier. Training used hard-label cross-entropy together with a KL-divergence term computed against smoothed targets (epsilon = 0.10; kl_weight = 1.5). Additional component-wise loss ablations, KAN pathway and spline-parameter sensitivity analyses, pure machine-learning baselines, and paired statistical tests were conducted. Results CLKAN-DBPred achieved 85.04 Acc, 0.7009 MCC, 0.8489 F1, and 0.9075 AUC in the reported fivefold CV evaluation and 81.76 Acc, 0.6352 MCC, 0.8163 F1, and 0.8905 AUC on PDB296. It obtained the highest AUC and MCC among the compared DBP predictors. The added analyses localized most of the KAN contribution to the spline pathway and showed limited sensitivity to the tested loss and spline settings. Against a direct XGBoost baseline on RFE-F7-1195, CLKAN-DBPred achieved stronger mean CV performance; paired independent-test differences in Acc, MCC, F1, and AUC were not significant. These results support CLKAN-DBPred as a competitive sequence-based framework for DBP prediction. All data and models are available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18023779.

title: Kernel variance-constrained partial least squares for robust nonlinear regression
abstract: In high-dimensional spectroscopic analysis, traditional Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression often suffers from overfitting and sensitivity to noise, especially when $p \gg n$. While Variance Constrained PLS (VCPLS) enhances stability through regularization, it remains limited by its linear assumption. This paper proposes a novel regression framework, Kernel Variance Constrained Partial Least Squares (KVCPLS). By integrating a variance-based constraint directly into the Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS), KVCPLS simultaneously addresses non-linearities and suppresses unstable spectral components. Theoretically, we demonstrate that KVCPLS achieves a tighter generalization error bound compared to standard KPLS and robust PLS variants. The computational complexity is optimized to $O(n^2p + n^3 + AIn^2)$ for training, ensuring suitability for high-throughput industrial tasks. Experimental results on five benchmark datasets indicate that KVCPLS consistently outperforms PLS, KPLS, and IRPLS, achieving an average reduction in RMSEP of 12.87\%. KVCPLS provides a robust and efficient solution for complex non-linear calibration, offering a solid theoretical foundation for real-time online monitoring in demanding industrial environments.

title: A comparative evaluation of deep learning and traditional clustering methods for automated point-of-care urinalysis
abstract: Accurate interpretation of urine test strips is vital for point-of-care (POC) diagnostics; however, manual readings are constrained by subjectivity, inter-observer variability, and inconsistent environmental conditions. This study presents a systematic comparison of three segmentation paradigms, K-means clustering, Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN), and the Segment Anything Model (SAM), for automated identification and delineation of reagent pads on ACON MISSION 10-parameter urine test strips. A dedicated portable imaging system was developed using a Raspberry Pi 4 with controlled LED-based illumination inside a fully enclosed 3D-printed chamber. Analytically prepared synthetic urine solutions (S1–S4) spanning clinically relevant concentration ranges for seven analytes, including glucose (500–2000mg/dL), protein (50–200mg/dL), and occult blood (0.75–3.0mg/dL), were used to generate a dataset of 120 images across five test conditions. All experiments were performed with five replicates per condition and five image captures per strip to assess reproducibility. From aggregate confusion-matrix analysis, SAM achieved 99.34% pixel-wise accuracy (± 0.15%), 94.34% precision, 87.71% recall, and an F1-score of 0.909, compared to K-means (96.57% accuracy, 52.69% precision, F1 = 0.622) and DBSCAN (94.56% accuracy, 38.46% precision, F1 = 0.513). The mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 83.32% (± 0.54%) further confirms SAM’s superior ability to delineate reagent pad boundaries with high fidelity. Statistical analysis revealed that SAM maintained a coefficient of variation below 0.5% across all concentration levels, demonstrating robust invariance to chromatic shifts. While this proof-of-concept utilizes synthetic samples under controlled conditions, the results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying transformer-based segmentation on low-cost embedded hardware for objective, automated urinalysis.

title: Bayesian-inspired fusion-based deep orthogonal decomposition strategy for quality-oriented fault detection
abstract: In modern industrial processes, quality-oriented fault detection is significantly challenged by the presence of multiple quality indicators, complex variable interactions, and the coexistence of quality-related and quality-unrelated variations. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel Bayesian-inspired Fusion-based Deep Orthogonal Decomposition (BF-DOD) strategy. First, a Bayesian-inspired mutual information fusion mechanism is developed to integrate the relevance scores across multiple quality indicators. This enables an effective partition of the original process variable space into distinct quality-related and quality-unrelated subspaces. Subsequently, a deep orthogonal decomposition framework is applied to hierarchically extract latent features from both partitioned spaces. Specifically, the quality-related subspace undergoes singular value decomposition based on cross-covariance structures to capture both dominant and subtle quality-sensitive variations. Concurrently, the quality-unrelated subspace is modeled using a deep residual principal component analysis strategy to recursively extract residual dynamics. During online monitoring, a unified Bayesian-inspired evidence-fusion mechanism heuristically combines the multi-layer monitoring indicators through Bayes-type normalization, thereby enhancing fault sensitivity, interpretability, and robustness. Finally, extensive case studies involving a numerical example, a three-phase flow process, and the Tennessee Eastman process, along with an ablation study, demonstrate that the proposed BF-DOD method exhibits competitive advantages. It successfully improves the detection of quality-related faults while effectively suppressing false alarms triggered by quality-unrelated disturbances.

title: Machine learning-driven analysis of Raman spectra for high-throughput characterization of functionalized graphene oxide composites
abstract: A combination of electrochemical exfoliation of graphite and machine learning was employed for the design of functionalized graphene oxide. From the Raman spectra of 31 samples modified with phenolic and amine compounds, the band area ratios SD/SG, SD′/SG, SD′′/SG, SD′/SD were calculated. The ensemble algorithms CatBoost and AdaBoost were applied to regression and classification tasks. CatBoost delivered the best overall performance: R2 = 0.97 ± 0.03 for defectiveness prediction and classification accuracy of 0.99 ± 0.01 (phenols 91%, amines 89%). The effectiveness depends on the nature of the modifier: AdaBoost predicts oxidation parameters more accurately for phenols (MAE = 0.19 ± 0.03), whereas CatBoost better predicts defectiveness for nitro compounds and heterocyclic amines (MAE = 0.14 ± 0.06). SHAP analysis confirmed the leading role of spectral descriptors, with the degree of oxidation dominating defectiveness prediction (mean |SHAP| = 0.63). Fundamental limitations were revealed for the amorphous phase descriptor, showing negative R2 under leave-one-group-out cross-validation (CatBoost: −0.12, AdaBoost: −0.48). The approach is promising for high-throughput analysis and the rational design of carbon composites.

title: Dual-branch spectral prediction network based on pearson feature marking
abstract: Aiming at the three core problems prevalent in deep learning models for near-infrared spectroscopic quantitative analysis, namely insufficient ability to distinguish the importance of wavelengths features, difficulty in collaborative extraction of global-local spectral information, and high redundancy of network structures, this paper proposes a Pearson feature marking-based dual-branch spectral prediction network (Mark-GLNet). This method first quantifies the correlation between each wavelengths feature and the prediction target via the Pearson correlation coefficient, screens key sensitive wavelengths, and effectively suppresses spectral redundant information; furthermore, a dual-branch parallel architecture consisting of Global Dependency Modeling (GDM) and Local Feature Mining (LFM) is constructed, in which the GDM module captures the long-range dependencies of spectral sequences through the multi-head self-attention mechanism, the LFM module extracts local fine-grained features of adjacent spectral wavelengths using multi-scale convolution, and collaborative optimization of global semantics and local details is finally realized through feature fusion. Systematic experiments on four public near-infrared spectral datasets from the pharmaceutical, agricultural and food fields demonstrate that Mark-GLNet exhibits excellent performance in both prediction accuracy and model robustness, and its dual-branch structure can effectively balance the global dependency characteristics and local feature details of spectral sequences. Ablation experiments further verify the independent effectiveness and synergistic enhancement effect of the GDM and LFM modules. The proposed network has a concise structure, favorable scalability and engineering practical value while maintaining high performance, providing a reliable deep learning solution for the quantitative analysis of high-dimensional complex spectral data.

title: Temporal representation enhanced latent predictive modeling for multivariate process monitoring
abstract: Fault detection in multivariate dynamic processes remains challenging because of strong variable correlations, temporal dependencies, and limited abnormal labels. Conventional statistical monitoring may be insufficient for weak dynamic deviations, while deep learning models do not always exploit compact latent representations or explicit temporal information. To address these issues, this study proposes a latent predictive monitoring framework that combines principal component analysis (PCA), learnable temporal encoding, and gated recurrent unit (GRU)-based multi-step prediction. Process measurements are projected into a compact PCA score space, augmented with explicit temporal representations, and monitored through prediction residuals between observed and predicted latent trajectories. The proposed framework is evaluated on the Benchmark Simulation Model No. 1 and further validated using industrial papermaking process data. On the BSM1 benchmark, the method achieved an average fault detection rate of 88.02 ± 2.73% with an average false alarm rate of 1.62 ± 0.15%, outperforming classical statistical methods and several deep learning baselines, particularly in slowly evolving and weakly distinguishable fault scenarios. The industrial case further demonstrated the transferability of the framework while revealing section-dependent false alarm behavior. These results indicate that integrating latent space projection with explicit temporal representation can improve the separability of prediction residuals in multivariate dynamic monitoring tasks.

title: Spatiotemporal learning with dynamic coordination for simultaneous classification and concentration regression of ozone and coexisting pollutant gases via MOS sensor arrays
abstract: Accurate monitoring of ground-level ozone and coexisting air pollutants remains challenging for low-cost metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) sensor arrays because their cross-sensitive responses are jointly governed by inter-sensor spatial correlations, gas-surface temporal dynamics, and task conflicts between gas identification and concentration regression. Here, we propose Spatiotemporal feature Decoupling with Dynamic task Coordination for Multi-Task Learning (STDC-MTL), an uncertainty-coordinated learning framework for simultaneous gas classification and concentration regression using MOS sensor-array signals. STDC-MTL explicitly integrates a hybrid spatiotemporal encoder for array-temporal correlation modeling, a dual-branch local-global feature learning module that separately captures neighborhood temporal variations and long-range response dependencies, and a Bayesian uncertainty-driven coordination mechanism for adaptive task balancing. Experimental results on a custom dataset of ozone, acetone, NO, NO2, and NH3 show that STDC-MTL achieves 100% classification accuracy and a concentration regression R2 of 0.998. More importantly, it reduces the mean absolute error (MAE) by 42.6% compared with the state-of-the-art Gaussian-TCN baseline, with an average normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) of 0.0138 and only 0.37 million parameters. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves quantitative prediction under cross-sensitive MOS responses while maintaining a lightweight architecture, providing an effective algorithmic strategy for intelligent air-pollutant sensing.

title: Testing for dilution effects in group testing
abstract: Group testing is widely used to improve screening efficiency in populations with low prevalence, but pooling may reduce assay sensitivity through dilution. Existing statistical work often incorporates this effect as a modeling assumption or design constraint, while the question of whether a dilution effect is present in a specific testing procedure is less often treated as a formal inferential problem. This paper develops a hypothesis testing framework for assessing dilution effects under a binary measurement error model. Dilution is represented by an increase in the group-specific false negative rate as pool size increases, with specificity assumed to remain stable across pool sizes. We derive closed-form estimators and one-sided test statistics for both unknown- and known-prevalence settings, using normal and Poisson approximations together with null-bootstrap critical-value calibration. Simulation studies show that the proposed procedures control type I error reasonably well and gain power as the dilution effect becomes stronger, although detection is more difficult under very low prevalence. Applications to infectious disease screening settings and SARS-CoV-2 pooled NAAT data illustrate how the framework can quantify evidence for reduced sensitivity under pooling.

title: Tail-aware Vis–NIR calibration of soil traits: Partial and sparse-group-lasso quantile regression versus PLS on the LUCAS library
abstract: This paper applies quantile-based statistical methodologies to visible and near-infrared (Vis–NIR) spectral data. Vis–NIR spectroscopy is the standard tool for rapid, non-destructive estimation of soil and agricultural traits, a task for which partial least squares (PLS) regression has been the gold standard for years. PLS, however, targets the conditional mean: it returns a single central value that is silent about the spread and tails of the conditional distribution. Its wavelength-level interpretations are also dense and tied to that mean. Yet when soil traits are skewed and heteroscedastic, predictive uncertainty varies sharply from sample to sample, so a description of the full conditional distribution — and a calibrated prediction interval — is more informative than a point estimate. We reframe spectral calibration as a high dimensional, multivariate quantile regression problem, benchmarking two methodologies against PLS on the LUCAS topsoil Vis–NIR library: fast partial quantile regression (FPQR) for prediction, and adaptive sparse group lasso quantile regression (ASGL-QR) for prediction and band selection. Across 100 Monte Carlo train–test partitions, both quantile methodologies matched PLS performance at the median. They additionally estimated the 10th and 90th percentiles, forming calibrated 80% prediction intervals with empirical coverage close to nominal. ASGL-QR band selection was stable across repetitions and revealed that the informative spectral region shifts toward the tail for right-skewed traits. These results show that quantile calibration delivers the full conditional distribution and a per-sample uncertainty statement at no cost to central accuracy.

title: Stationary-based self-supervised contrastive learning for soft measurement of free Calcium Oxide
abstract: Free Calcium Oxide (f-CaO) content in cement clinker is a pivotal quality indicator for cement production, and accurate detection of this content is considered the core of intelligent control for cement calcination processes. However, the scarcity of labeled f-CaO samples limits the performance of traditional soft measurement models. More critically, the stationary of the cement production process exerts a dominant impact on clinker f-CaO content, where non-stationary dynamic fluctuations in the cement production process directly affect the variation of f-CaO content. Nevertheless, existing self-supervised contrastive learning methods developed for industrial soft measurement are rarely tailored to the non-stationary of cement production processes, leading to learned features that deviate from actual production state characteristics and fail to cope with complex dynamic process variations. To address these problems, a stationary-based Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning (SSCL) method for f-CaO soft measurement is proposed. Stationary labels and scores are constructed via a dynamically adjustable sliding window and the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test. A multi-channel attention and Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) feature extraction module is designed to capture variable coupling and long-range temporal dependencies, and a stationary weighted contrastive loss function is developed to guide the learning of robust stationary features. Experimental results obtained from real industrial cement production data verify that the proposed SSCL model achieves optimal prediction performance. The proposed model is demonstrated to outperform comparative models, and prediction accuracy and generalization ability are significantly improved under limited labeled data conditions.

title: nirs4all: Canonical, content-addressed workflows for reproducible near-infrared calibration
abstract: A published near-infrared calibration is rarely a fully reproducible one. Its reported error depends on analyst decisions about signal representation, scatter correction, replicate handling, validation design, latent-variable selection, aggregation and model family. These decisions usually survive as scripts and output files rather than as one re-executable calibration object. We present nirs4all, an open-source Python system for making that object explicit. The contribution is a computer technique for chemometric reproducibility, not a new calibration algorithm. nirs4all records preprocessing and latent-variable search as canonical workflow declarations, links predictions and fitted artefacts back to the exact fold, chain and dataset hashes that produced them, and makes validation semantics such as signal type, replicate-grouped splitting and specimen-level aggregation first-class. A controller layer lets standard Python estimators and near-infrared operators share this workflow, provenance and deployment contract. On public datasets we show deterministic representation and verifiable provenance under a pinned environment, held-out partial-least-squares reporting isolated from selection, auditable replicate policy, and bounded operational cost. This is reproducibility of the declaration and lineage; strict bitwise numerical replay still requires a pinned environment or container. nirs4all is available at https://github.com/GBeurier/nirs4all (pip install nirs4all, AGPL-3.0-or-later primary public licence).

title: Leakage-safe benchmarking of conventional chemometric and deep learning models for food NIR spectroscopy regression
abstract: Near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy is widely used in food systems for rapid, non-destructive estimation of compositional and quality attributes. Although machine-learning and deep-learning models are increasingly reported for spectral regression, practical model selection is often hindered by heterogeneous validation setups and the risk of information leakage during preprocessing and tuning. In this study, we provide a leakage-safe benchmark across nine food-related regression tasks spanning different sample sizes and spectral dimensionalities. Conventional chemometric and regression baselines (partial least squares regression, ridge regression, and support vector regression) are compared with lightweight deep-learning baselines (a shallow artificial neural network and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network) under a unified leakage-safe evaluation framework combining nested cross-validation with acomplementary fixed held-out test-set assessment, fold-wise preprocessing, and repeated training for stochastic models. Performance is summarized primarily using prediction error (RMSE in nested cross-validation and RMSEP on the held-out test set), while the coefficient of determination is retained as a secondary descriptive measure, complemented by cross-validation and fixed held-out-test learning-curve analyses together with model-complexity analysis. Across both validation analyses, ridge regression achieved the largest number of numerical task-level wins, while partial least squares regression and support vector regression remained competitive across multiple tasks. Paired randomization tests following van der Voet further showed that some small numerical differences between models were not statistically distinguishable. Artificial neural network and one-dimensional convolutional neural network baselines did not provide a reliable generalization advantage and showed greater variability in some data-limited settings. From a food-measurement perspective, these findings indicate that well-validated conventional models remain a strong default for routine NIR calibration workflows and non-destructive quality assessment. Deep learning appears most justified when calibration settings provide larger datasets, stronger experimental control, or spectroscopy-specific inductive bias that can translate added model complexity into practical measurement gains. Overall, this study serves as a controlled benchmark and reference for model selection under realistic food-spectroscopy data regimes.

title: Diffusion regulated particle filtering via Bayesian transfer learning for nonlinear state estimation
abstract: Particle filtering is effective for nonlinear Bayesian state estimation, but uncertain model dynamics may bias particle propagation and degrade posterior approximation. To address this issue, this paper proposes a diffusion regulated particle filter via Bayesian transfer learning for nonlinear state estimation under model uncertainty. Different from existing robust particle filters that only exploit target domain information, the proposed method incorporates predictive knowledge from a related source domain and adaptively regulates its contribution according to target measurements. The source predictive distribution is represented by weighted particles and transformed into a kernelized transferable density. A positive tuning factor is introduced to regulate the diffusion degree of this transferred particle density, thereby extending the covariance scaling mechanism from Gaussian transfer estimation to nonparametric particle based Bayesian filtering. The tuning factor is inferred online from target measurements under a variational Bayesian criterion, so that source knowledge is strengthened when it is consistent with the target data and weakened when negative transfer may occur. Compared with conventional robust particle filters, the proposed approach provides an adaptive mechanism for balancing source predictive knowledge and target measurements, thereby improving posterior approximation accuracy without requiring an exact target dynamic model. The resulting estimator preserves the essential transfer mechanism of covariance regulated Gaussian prediction while removing the linearity and Gaussian restrictions. Theoretical analysis is provided to establish boundedness of the transfer corrected importance weights and convergence of the empirical posterior approximation. Simulation studies on nonlinear target tracking and a nonlinear torsion system demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method under uncertain dynamics and measurement models.

title: State-of-the-art review of graph neural networks for chemical process fault detection and diagnosis: Applications and implementation guidelines
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) offer a novel and effective approach for fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) in highly interconnected chemical process systems. By explicitly modeling relational and structural dependencies among process variables and units, GNNs provide a powerful alternative to conventional deep learning methods, which often overlook the intrinsic connectivity of chemical plants. This review presents a comprehensive overview of state-of-the-art GNN-based FDD frameworks and their applications in chemical process industries. We first introduce the fundamental principles and architectures of GNNs, including graph convolutional networks, recurrent GNNs, graph autoencoders, spatiotemporal GNNs, graph attention networks, semi-supervised GNNs, and multi-scale GNNs, emphasizing their ability to capture fault propagation pathways and inter-unit interactions. Recent studies are surveyed, highlighting the superior performance of GNNs in fault detection and localization. Key advantages, including relational learning, early fault identification, and message-passing mechanisms for local and global behavior, are discussed. Practical implementation guidelines are provided, including graph-based process representation, graph representation learning, model training strategies, and online deployment. Industrial case studies, particularly distillation columns, demonstrate how graph-structured modeling enhances fault detection, localization, and interpretability. Finally, current limitations such as limited industrial adoption, interpretability challenges, and a lack of standardized implementation practices are outlined, and future research directions are proposed to develop robust, scalable, and explainable GNN-based FDD frameworks for Industry 4.0 chemical plants.
