title: Inversion soil organic matter using transformer based on partitioned attention mechanism with ZY1-02D hyperspectral
abstract: This study focuses on the highland red soil area in Dongchuan District, Kunming City, Yunnan Province. Using ZY1-02D satellite hyperspectral imagery as the data source, a total of 266 soil samples were collected, and the dataset was divided into a training set and a testing set in a 7:3 ratio. To address the issues of high noise and complexity in remote sensing data, we jointly applied direct standardization (DS) and piecewise direct standardization (PDS) for spectral correction. Furthermore, we combined standard normal variate (SNV), Savitzky-Golay (SG) smoothing, and first derivative (FD) preprocessing, along with competitive adaptive reweighted sampling (CARS) for feature band selection. On this basis, we proposed a partition-based deep learning model, SpecPAT-Net, for soil organic matter (SOM) content inversion. The model employs a lightweight CNN-Transformer hybrid architecture, incorporating a partition attention mechanism and a partition-weighted loss function to focus on critical spectral regions. The results demonstrate that the SpecPAT-Net model achieves optimal predictive performance on the test set: R2 = 0.5263, RMSE = 12.2293 g/kg, RPD = 1.4529, and RPIQ = 1.8644. Compared to the unimproved Transformer baseline model, R2 is improved by 0.2434, RMSE is reduced by 2.8176, and RPD and RPIQ are increased by 0.2720 and 0.3491, respectively. Furthermore, SHAP analysis was employed to interpret the 10 sensitive bands associated with SOM, and the proposed inversion model was used to predict the spatial distribution of SOM in the study area. The inversion results reveal that SOM in the study area exhibits a patchy distribution pattern, with higher contents in mid-to-high elevation gentle slope zones and lower contents in river valleys and agricultural reclamation areas. This spatial pattern is closely related to vegetation cover, topographic slope, and climatic conditions. This study provides a new framework for large-scale remote sensing inversion of SOM in mountainous red soils of the Yunnan Plateau. Codes are available at https://github.com/Liu641aaa/SpecPAT-Net.

title: Multivariate evaluation of the influence of soil perturbation on REE distribution and accumulation patterns in plants
abstract: The demand for Rare Earth Elements (REE) is rapidly increasing due to their widespread use in advanced technologies, making them emerging environmental contaminants. Although non-essential for plants, REE can accumulate in plant tissues and transfer through trophic levels, raising questions about how plants respond to changes in soil REE composition. This study investigates the effect of soil REE perturbation on their accumulation and distribution in Vitis vinifera L .. To this end, a full factorial (3 2 ) experimental design was implemented, combining three levels of treatment (control, low, high) with three sampling positions (soil, roots, leaves). The contribution of treatment, position, and their interaction was assessed using ANOVA–Simultaneous Component Analysis (ASCA) with permutation-based significance testing. The consistency of the inferred results was evaluated across different data processing strategies. First, inter-individual dispersion among experimental replicates was minimized through an orthogonal projection. Second, a dedicated ASCA without soil samples was performed to highlight if the significance of the position effect was driven by the artificial addition of REE. Results showed that treatment was the main driver of REE accumulation. Notably, the interaction between treatment and position explained more variance than position alone, indicating that REE distribution across compartments is modulated by soil enrichment level. The proposed approach offers a robust framework for investigating complex soil–plant interactions and supports targeted sampling strategies for field-based REE monitoring.

title: Confidence intervals for Partial Least Squares: A second-order Edgeworth expansion approach
abstract: Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression is a cornerstone of chemometric modeling, particularly for multivariate calibration where predictors (e.g., spectral channels) exhibit extreme multicollinearity. While point estimation is well-established, reliable inference in finite samples remains problematic due to the nonlinear nature of the PLS estimator. This paper introduces a novel second-order accurate confidence interval based on a bootstrap-calibrated Edgeworth expansion. Unlike first-order asymptotic methods, our approach explicitly corrects for the skewness and kurtosis inherent in PLS distributions under strong collinearity. Using an extensive Monte Carlo framework, we show that the proposed Edgeworth bootstrap method provides the most accurate coverage, especially in small samples and under strong collinearity. These findings offer practical guidance for applied researchers conducting inference in PLS regression.

title: Uniqueness in multivariate curve resolution, re-tuned
abstract: There are many misunderstandings about the term and interpretation of uniqueness in multivariate curve resolution tasks. In CAC2026 Tarragona, it turned out that even mathematicians do not properly construe Manne’s theorems. So we decided to provide this re-tuned summary, using several original quotes, their explanations, and newly created illustrative figures to get the points across. This contribution then explicitly offers the following: (i) a unified interpretation of Manne’s conditions, DBU, GRU, minimal constrained duality, and particular-solution-based criteria; (ii) newly constructed visual illustrations, including a counterexample; and (iii) a practical workflow for diagnosing uniqueness in nonnegative bilinear MCR.

title: Instrument-shift-informed source-domain augmentation for calibration transfer in near-infrared spectroscopy
abstract: Differences in instrumental response can degrade a calibration model when it is transferred to another instrument. We propose instrument-shift-informed source-domain augmentation (ISSA), which uses a limited number of paired spectra to adapt a source calibration model without target-domain reference values during transfer-set construction, parameter selection, or model fitting. Source-space PCA-KS preselects M candidates for paired measurement, and unlabeled screening retains K representative inter-instrument differences. Scaled convex perturbations generated from these differences augment the source spectra used to train a partial least squares regression model. ISSA was evaluated on the Corn, Tablet, and Wheat datasets across 10 transfer directions and six budgets (K=5–30; M=7–38). It reduced validation RMSE relative to direct application of the source model in all 60 direction–budget combinations, with a mean reduction of 73.3%. Thus, ISSA improved cross-instrument prediction under the pointwise-aligned, limited-pair conditions studied here without correcting target spectra at prediction time.

title: Chemometrics Web App: Synthetic Sampling
abstract: ABSTRACT This work reports the release and usability of the Chemometrics Web App: Synthetic Sampling (CWA: SS), an open-source application developed in the R environment with the Shiny package to address class imbalance in analytical and chemometric datasets. By leveraging the reticulate package, CWA: SS integrates Python’s imbalanced-learn library into a unified graphical user interface made on the basis of Shiny package on posit platform, offering 16 sampling algorithms, including oversampling, undersampling, and hybrid methods. A fundamental contribution of this application is the implementation of a systematized strategy to evaluate the efficiency and quality of synthetic sampling before the predictive modeling phase. This diagnostic module incorporates multivariate tools, such as Generalized Procrustes Analysis, PERMANOVA, Hotelling T 2 , and spectral profile comparisons, to ensure that synthetic data preserve original chemical and structural relationships without introducing artifacts or bias to the synthetic data. The application’s performance was validated through two distinct scenarios: a multiclass QSAR dataset, and a portable NIR spectral dataset (900–1700 nm) used to identify the integrity of Jatobá fruit. The results demonstrate that CWA: SS effectively handles multiclass problems and maintains the integrity of complex spectral profiles. The software is accessible via standalone executable, or cloud-based hosting through the LTAP website ( https://www.ltapuerj.com.br ), providing a flexible and user-friendly tool for both laboratory and field-based research without the need for programming expertise.

title: Cross-study shift defines the reliability limits of FTIR polymer classification
abstract: Automated Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) classifiers for microplastics are often evaluated by randomly splitting spectra pooled from several studies, although deployment requires transfer to new sources. We harmonized 4,783 labelled spectra from four independent studies and compared a study-mixed random split with leave-one-study-out (LOSO) evaluation. We then examined task composition, source-associated structure, nested deep and domain-oriented models, external reference-library pooling, and selective prediction on locked domains. XGBoost achieved random-split macro-F1 of 0.972 but equal-study present-class LOSO macro-F1 of 0.672. The gap was class- and source-dependent: PE/PP transfer remained strong, whereas adding PET and PS reopened most of the shared-fold deficit despite adequate class support. Polymer class dominated the global geometry of the harmonized data, yet source study remained highly predictable, including within PE and PP. Position-aware convolutional, self-supervised and domain-adversarial configurations did not consistently outperform XGBoost, and external libraries produced non-monotonic effects, indicating that directional compatibility mattered more than library size. A maximum-probability threshold selected only from inner study holdouts identified lower-risk subsets on locked De Frond and Open Specy domains, although coverage was domain-dependent. These results support a practical trust framework for multi-source FTIR classification: validate by study, report fold- and support-aware metrics, screen external libraries for compatibility, and defer spectra outside the model's reliable operating region.

title: BRing Harmony to oscillatory systems: A Hue–SSWT approach for descriptor extraction from non-stationary chromogenic oscillations
abstract: Oscillatory chemical reactions often exhibit time-dependent period variations, limiting the usefulness of conventional scalar period descriptors for non-stationary signals. Here, we combine Hue-based digital imaging with the synchrosqueezed wavelet transform (SSWT) to extract operational descriptors from chromogenic oscillations, including frequency-drift turning points, harmonic-transition behavior, and symmetry-related temporal indices. Surrogate-signal analysis demonstrated recovery of predefined structural features under controlled waveform conditions. Applied to the Briggs–Rauscher reaction, the method revealed that starch and Mn(II) affect different aspects of oscillatory dynamics, including persistence, frequency drift, harmonic organization, and waveform symmetry. Replicate-level analysis further showed that these descriptors exhibit distinct condition-dependent response patterns, providing complementary information. The Hue–SSWT workflow therefore provides a methodological proof of concept for compact and interpretable characterization of non-stationary chromogenic oscillations.

title: An adaptive multimodal fusion framework based on hyperspectral imaging for geographical origin authentication of botanical products: A case study of Forsythiae Fructus
abstract: Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) simultaneously provides spectral and spatial information, thus offering a promising tool for geographical origin authentication of botanical products. However, the respective contributions and complementarity of various modalities remain inadequately understood, making it difficult to effectively integrate their complementary information. This study aimed to evaluate the respective contributions of spectral and image modalities to the geographical origin authentication of Forsythiae Fructus (a traditional Chinese medicine) and develop an adaptive fusion strategy for integrating these complementary modalities. Samples were collected from four major production regions in China, and their HSI data were acquired. A transfer learning-based Mask Region-based Convolutional Neural Network (Mask R-CNN) was employed to automatically extract regions of interest (ROIs) from individual fruits. Single-modality models based on spectral, shallow-image (textural), and deep-image features, together with early fusion models and an adaptive spectral–deep-image mid-level fusion model, were systematically established and compared. Among the single-modality models, the spectral modality achieved the best classification performance. However, the image modalities captured discriminative characteristics different from those of the spectral modality, thereby providing complementary information for multimodal fusion. The early fusion model combining spectral and shallow-image features achieved an accuracy of 0.9093, whereas the proposed adaptive spectral–deep-image fusion model achieved the highest accuracy of 0.9402. Ablation experiments further demonstrated that the adaptive mechanism enhanced fusion effectiveness and improved the ability of the model to capture inter-sample differences. These findings clarify the complementary contributions of different HSI modalities and establish an adaptive framework for geographical origin authentication of botanical products.

title: Robust preprocessing and peak extraction method for machine learning-based classification of surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy
abstract: Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) provides sensitive molecular detection, but spectra acquired from heterogeneous substrates can span logarithmic intensity ranges. This nuisance variation can dominate distances and fitted decision functions even when peak locations remain informative. We present Blurred Laplacian Peak Extraction (BLaPE), a scale-selective preprocessing transform that smooths a spectrum at an expected peak-width scale, computes its rectified negative Laplacian, and normalizes the curvature response by signal magnitude. The resulting features encode peak presence within the [0, 1] range. We evaluated the method using 17,875 SERS spectra from 376 dyed and aged organic dye specimens prepared across substrate, dye, mordant, and aging factors. For dye identification, BLaPE reduced the classification error from 26.31 to 8.38% for cosine k-nearest neighbors and from 24.28 to 9.09% for random forest. Improvements were smaller for higher-capacity neural networks, and conventional scaling remained comparable or better for some of these models. An independent public Raman benchmark reproduced this model-capacity-dependent pattern, with the largest gains for instance-based and classical classifiers. BLaPE therefore provides an interpretable peak-centered representation for classification problems in which large spectral intensity variation would otherwise dominate the input.

title: Rapid profiling of relative chemical distribution patterns of major constituents in whole green Amazonian Robusta beans by near-infrared spectral resolution
abstract: To address the limited chemical data on Amazonian Robusta, this proof-of-concept study evaluated the relative distribution patterns of trigonelline, caffeine, carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and organic acids in green coffee beans from Rondônia produced by indigenous farmers, Acre, and Amazonas. Analyses were conducted directly on whole beans using near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy, providing a rapid and minimally invasive approach, while analytical standards of coffee constituents were similarly analyzed and incorporated into the resolution process as chemically oriented initial estimates. Principal component analysis revealed substantial overlap among the coffee samples, supporting the subsequent application of multivariate curve resolution–alternating least squares (MCR-ALS) to obtain more interpretable chemical information. MCR-ALS resolved spectral profiles associated with the target constituents and revealed distinct relative chemical distribution patterns among coffee samples, mainly for chlorogenic acids, caffeic acid, sucrose, casein, and lipids. These results provide preliminary comparisons of compositional trends that may be associated with origin-related chemical patterns among Amazonian regional coffees, as well as correlations between relative concentration profiles and overall sensory quality. The use of chemically oriented initial estimates enabled the resolution and interpretation of complex coffee spectra as multiple relative chemical profiles directly from whole coffee beans.

title: IC-DA chemometric tool coupled to MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for organic spices and herbs evaluation
abstract: The consumer demand for healthy food contributes to the growth of organic food consumption, which in turn increases the price of this type of food. Among the organic products, spices and herbs stand out for their characteristic flavor and bioactive compounds. Considering the lack of applications of the analytical technique based on Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption Ionization Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry (MALDI-TOF-MS) in the evaluation of organic foods, as well as the absence of Independent Components Discriminant Analysis (IC-DA) chemometric application in organic food discrimination, this work aims to propose a method for the discrimination of organic and non-organic cinnamon, mint, oregano, and rosemary using MALDI-TOF-MS coupled with IC-DA. The method proved effective in differentiating between organic and conventional spices, advancing our understanding of the classes of compounds that distinguish these two farming practices. The results highlight the potential of this innovative approach for rapid screening and evaluation of organic food through high-throughput analysis, with minimal sample preparation and relatively low per-sample costs, supporting its suitability for routine applications in organic food authentication.

title: Transfer calibrated mode probability learning for multiple model state estimation in dynamic process monitoring
abstract: This paper studies multiple model state estimation for dynamic processes operating under switching regimes, model mismatch, and uncertain mode transitions. Such situations frequently arise in process monitoring, soft sensing, and laboratory dynamic systems, where different operating modes may coexist and the available model set is often imperfect. Classical interacting multiple model (IMM) estimators update mode probabilities only through likelihood-based Bayesian recursion. When the transition matrix is misspecified or the local process models are inaccurate, the resulting mode posterior may remain diffuse or assign excessive probability to an incorrect operating mode, leading to degraded state estimation performance. To address this problem, a transfer-calibrated mode probability learning scheme is proposed. The conventional IMM mode posterior is treated as a baseline and is corrected by a transferable compatibility prior constructed from innovation statistics, fused-state consistency, and transition information. The calibrated mode probabilities are obtained in a closed form through probability reweighting, while the per-mode Kalman filters and the original multiple-model structure remain unchanged. A KL-based calibration strength is further introduced to control the deviation from the IMM baseline and reduce the risk of negative transfer. Probabilistic analysis shows that, under moderate compatibility assumptions, the calibrated posterior increases the concentration of probability on the true operating mode. Simulation studies on a switching dynamic process, a one-degree-of-freedom laboratory torsion system, and a multimode continuous stirred-tank reactor demonstrate that the proposed method improves state estimation and mode identification under model mismatch, with more reliable mode probability learning than the conventional IMM.

title: Overcoming intra-root heterogeneity in astragali radix through multi-segment LIBS spectral fusion for improved mineral element quantification
abstract: Intra-root heterogeneity poses a major challenge for the quality control of Astragalus membranaceus (Astragali Radix). Conventional assessment typically relies on a single representative segment, which overlooks the inherent structural variations and fails to capture the holistic profile of the entire organ. In this study, we demonstrate that the heterogeneity is predominantly radial, between phloem and xylem, rather than longitudinal. Each root was divided into four key segments (upper/lower × phloem/xylem) and analyzed by laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS). Principal component analysis combined with Mahalanobis distance (PCA-MD) and partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) revealed strong spectral differences between phloem and xylem, which were validated by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) elemental analysis. To overcome tissue-specific bias, low-level and mid-level data fusion strategies were developed. A supervised fusion strategy combining variable importance in projection (VIP) and competitive adaptive reweighted sampling (CARS) was used to select key features from each tissue before concatenation. The fused spectra, correlated with a mass-weighted average of the whole-root elemental content, demonstrated significantly superior predictive performance for K and Ca (PLSR: R2 = 0.841 and 0.846, respectively) compared to any single segment. K and Ca serve as demonstration targets for methodological validation rather than comprehensive markers of medicinal efficacy, thereby facilitating robust model development. Our findings offer a more information-rich approach for spectroscopic quantification of mineral elements in spatially heterogeneous medicinal roots, and in future work this strategy could be extended to bioactive compounds such as saponins, flavonoids and polysaccharides.

title: Leakage-aware window-based chemometric monitoring for event-level anomaly detection in batch distillation
abstract: Batch distillation processes exhibit dynamic and phase-dependent behavior, making anomaly detection a challenging task in multivariate process monitoring. This study proposes a leakage-aware window-based chemometric learning framework for event-level anomaly detection using sensor and actuator time series. The framework transforms multivariate process trajectories into temporal windows described by local statistical descriptors, compares several supervised classifiers, and evaluates predictive performance using stratified grouped cross-validation by experiment. This validation strategy keeps all windows from the same experiment within the same fold, reducing information leakage and allowing model performance to be assessed on unseen experiments. The final analytical dataset contained 11,413 windows, 217 predictor variables, and 119 experiments. Tree-based ensemble models achieved the strongest window-level performance. Extra Trees obtained the highest F1-score, 0.655 ± 0.047, while Random Forest achieved a comparable F1-score, 0.653 ± 0.037, with ROC-AUC 0.862 ± 0.022 and average precision 0.719 ± 0.083. At the experiment level, Random Forest provided the best operational trade-off, detecting 75 out of 81 anomalous experiments while producing false alarms in 15 out of 38 normal experiments. Threshold-based and temporal persistence-based alert rules were analyzed to study the balance between sensitivity and false alarm reduction. Permutation importance showed that temperature-related variables, pressure-related variables, and actuator signals contributed to anomaly detection, with range and standard deviation emerging as the most informative window descriptors. These results indicate that reliable anomaly detection in batch processes requires leakage-aware validation, event-level evaluation, temporal alert analysis, and interpretable assessment of local chemometric descriptors.

title: GA-DB-CNN driven metasurface-enhanced terahertz spectroscopy: A framework for trace multi-component analysis
abstract: For the need of rapid, non-destructive detection of trace organic mixtures, terahertz spectroscopy integrated with metasurface enhancement offers unique advantages. However, existing machine learning methods face challenges in accuracy and robustness for qualitative identification and quantitative analysis when dealing with severely overlapping mixture spectra. This study proposes a Gated Attention-Dual Branch Convolutional Neural Network (GA-DB-CNN) framework. The framework achieves simultaneous component identification and concentration prediction, with an overall identification accuracy of 96.2% and coefficients of determination (R2) exceeding 0.85 for all three analytes, demonstrating the methodological potential for extensibility to trace multi-component analysis.

title: Artificial neural network and response surface methodology-driven optimization of sustainable extraction, chromatographic quantification and bioactivity evaluation of flavonoids in Rhizophora apiculata leaves across Vietnamese mangrove ecosystems
abstract: Mangrove ecosystems contain chemically diverse plant species rich in natural products; however, comprehensive phytochemical profiles, especially of Rhizophora apiculata Blume, remain limited. This study developed a comprehensive workflow for sustainable extraction, chromatographic quantification, and bioactivity evaluation of flavonoids from R. apiculata leaves collected across Vietnamese mangrove ecosystems. Four extraction parameters were optimized using response surface methodology (RSM) and artificial neural network (ANN) to maximize total flavonoid content (TFC) and its antioxidant activity. Ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE) using 70% ethanol, solid-liquid ratio of 1:20, 35 °C and 60 min was identified as the optimum. ANN and RSM produced comparable predictions, while ANN provided a useful complementary nonlinear modeling approach within the design investigated. The validated HPLC method for rutin and quercetin showed excellent linearity, with LOD/LOQ values of 17.8226/54.0080 μg/mL for rutin, and 0.3352/1.0156 μg/mL for quercetin, along with recoveries of 95.10–100.80% and 94.40–101.94%, respectively. The highest TFC, rutin, and quercetin (mg/g) reached 34.6871 (Ben Tre), 5.9334 (Can Gio), and 0.1231 (Vung Tau), respectively. Bioactivity patterns were associated with variations in flavonoid content and may additionally reflect contributions from other phytochemical constituents detected in the LC-MS profile. Antioxidant activity varied among geographical samples, with IC50 values ranging from 134.21 μg/mL (Can Gio) to 306.94 μg/mL (Tien Giang). Ben Tre leaves exhibited the strongest antibacterial activity against MSSA and MRSA, with MIC values of 12.5 and 6.25 mg/mL, respectively, and concentration-dependent killing behavior in time-kill assays. Greenness assessment (Eco-Scale >75; AGREE 0.69; BAGI 0.63; GAPI >75) confirmed the reliability and sustainability of UAE–HPLC strategy. These findings highlight the potential of AI-assisted chemometric modeling for sustainable quality assessment of mangrove-derived phytochemicals.

title: Integrated chemometric pipeline combining point-based X-ray fluorescence and chromatic-textural fractal metrics for cultural heritage analysis
abstract: Portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) spectroscopy enables precise, non-destructive elemental characterization of cultural heritage materials, yet traditional point-based measurements inherently overlook the spatial and chromatic variability of the pictorial application. To address this limitation, a data-driven chemometric pipeline was developed to integrate high-dimensional compositional data (pXRF) with chromatic and textural descriptors derived from multidimensional fractal analysis (FD-RGB and FD-Gray). Using a historical copy of Raphael's “The Transfiguration” as a comprehensive case study, 165 localized XRF elemental profiles were statistically associated with fractal descriptors extracted from high-resolution digital patches. This single-painting case study is framed as a proof of concept, and the resulting pigment-texture relationships are interpreted as preliminary and case-dependent rather than as universal thresholds. Rank-based correlation analysis, Kruskal-Wallis tests, Dunn post-hoc comparisons with Benjamini–Hochberg control across contrasts, and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) were applied to evaluate the multivariate behavior of specific major chemical families. The integrated analysis demonstrates a directional mathematical decoupling of luminance-based texture from chromatic complexity. Results indicate that luminance variations (quantified via FD-Gray) show minimal dependence on the localized chemical palette, while multiscale chromatic variance (FD-RGB) effectively discriminates between opaque and multilayered applications (|ρ| ≈ 0.17-0.22; several remained significant under within-descriptor false-discovery-rate control). Specifically, pigments defining high-hiding matrices (based on Pb, Sn) reduce the chromatic complexity (FD-RGB), whereas pigments historically associated with chiaroscuro and translucent glazes (based on Hg, Mn, Ca) markedly increase this fractal complexity. In a dominance-based variance analysis, FD-RGB differed across groups ( p = 0.018; η 2 = 0.222), while Dunn pairwise differences were nominal at the unadjusted level. PCA of the standardized matrix (18 elemental variables + FD-RGB/FD-Gray) showed that PC1 (33.03%) aligns with an opacity-translucency continuum driven by Pb, Ba, As, Cd, and Sb, opposed to FD-RGB, whereas PC2 (11.77%) separates cool (based on Co, Ni, and Cu) from warm/shadow domains (based on Ca, Mn, Fe, and Hg) with FD-RGB loading negatively. This data-driven framework transforms raw chemical data into objective art-technical knowledge, demonstrating its capacity to characterize painterly execution beyond pigment concentration, and offering a robust new computational tool for Heritage Science.

title: Out-of-fold-guided adaptive local residual calibration for near-infrared spectroscopic regression: Soil organic matter prediction and cross-domain validation
abstract: Soil organic matter (SOM) is an important indicator of soil fertility and nutrient cycling, and near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy enables its rapid and non-destructive quantitative analysis. However, even a well-performing global calibration model may retain structured residual errors for subsets of samples. To address this issue, we propose an out-of-fold-guided adaptive local residual calibration framework (OOF-ALRC) that corrects the remaining errors of an established global predictor without replacing it. Classical partial least squares regression (PLS) was used as a linear chemometric baseline, whereas PLS-SVR served as the global nonlinear calibration model. Repeated K-fold out-of-fold prediction was used to generate cross-fitted residuals within the calibration domain, reducing the optimistic bias associated with training residuals. For a new sample, neighboring calibration samples were identified in PCA latent-variable space, and their OOF residuals were used to estimate a local correction to the global prediction. On the fixed confirmatory soil test set, R2 increased from 0.7302 for PLS to 0.8021 for Global PLS-SVR and 0.8254 for OOF-ALRC. Relative to Global PLS-SVR, OOF-ALRC reduced RMSE and MAE by 6.07% and 13.16%, respectively, to 3.8640 and 2.8505 g kg−1. Permutation-based residual analysis and model-simplification experiments further supported PCA latent-variable neighborhoods for local residual calibration. Across six additional non-soil NIR regression tasks, OOF-ALRC yielded additional numerical improvements in five, whereas one cross-season task showed little further benefit. These results support OOF-ALRC as a conditional residual-correction strategy built on an established global calibration model rather than as a general replacement for conventional chemometric calibration.

title: TabNet versus chemometrics in NIR and Raman spectroscopy: Robustness and interpretability
abstract: Deep tabular models such as TabNet combine nonlinear prediction with built-in feature attention, but their performance relative to classical chemometric methods may depend strongly on how hierarchically structured spectroscopic data are evaluated. We compare TabNet with representative chemometric and machine-learning baselines on three tasks spanning NIR regression, NIR binary classification and Raman multi-class classification. To assess generalization beyond familiar samples and batches, the evaluation uses population- and season-disjoint validation for the mango NIR data and similarity-group-disjoint validation for the Fritillaria Raman data, while pooled random splitting is retained as a within-distribution reference. Under that reference TabNet remains close to PLS on mango dry-matter regression (R2 = 0.874 ± 0.017 for individual fits versus 0.891 for PLS with cross-validation-selected components), but the ranking changes under the stricter protocols, where the classical methods show greater stability under population shift. Seed ensembling, however, markedly improves TabNet robustness: on mango dry-matter regression a seven-model ensemble reaches R2 = 0.795, close to PLS at 0.819, and on the 804-spectrum Fritillaria Raman task it reaches 0.992 accuracy, matching the best classical result. Mango type classification remains more favourable to LDA under population-disjoint evaluation. Cross-seed consensus attention maps are reproducible at the band level and point to the water and carbohydrate overtone region in the NIR data and to a carbonyl-related region in the Raman data. Overall, group-aware evaluation is critical for spectroscopic machine learning, and seed ensembling can substantially improve the robustness of TabNet while preserving its built-in interpretability.

title: Adaptive saliency cascade network for efficient multiclass classification of multi-source brain MRI data
abstract: Multi-source brain MRI classification is complicated by subtle inter-class similarities and source-dependent variation in contrast, orientation, field of view, and acquisition protocol. These factors can obscure disease-related cues and make apparent performance sensitive to the evaluation design. This study proposes the Adaptive Saliency Cascade Network (ASC-Net), a compact four-stage classifier built from Adaptive Saliency Conduit (ASC) blocks that combine efficient additive attention with gated feature modulation for selective spatial and channel refinement. ASC-Net achieved 99.34% accuracy and a 99.36% macro F1-score on the randomly partitioned ND-5 image-level benchmark, exceeding the strongest directly trained comparator by 0.71 and 0.69 percentage points, respectively, with 11.15 million parameters and 4.19 GFLOPs. Because patient or examination identifiers are unavailable for the consolidated ND-5 sources, this internal result is interpreted strictly as an image-level benchmark. Generalization was examined separately on BDNeuro-MRI, an external dataset-level cohort excluded from training, validation, checkpoint selection, and hyperparameter decisions. Without retraining or adaptation, ASC-Net obtained 98.70% accuracy (95% CI: 98.38%–98.96%) and a 98.61% macro F1-score (95% CI: 98.28%–98.92%) on 5941 external images. In post-hoc exploratory image-level comparisons, the macro F1 difference from the strongest external comparator remained significant after Holm correction (pHolm=0.0004). Patient- or case-level identifiers were unavailable for clustered external resampling, so the reported confidence intervals and p values quantify image-level rather than patient-level uncertainty. Ablation analysis preserved the same component ordering on ND-5 and BDNeuro-MRI. These findings support cross-dataset transfer while retaining the need for verified patient-level and prospective clinical validation.

title: Process-aware inference of biomedical Raman spectra classification
abstract: The evaluation of classification models is mostly based on accuracy. However, biomedical data often contain heterogeneous, spatially or spectrally distributed contributions that may provide partially conflicting evidence during classification. In such settings, analyzing how this evidence is reconciled during inference can complement conventional performance metrics and provide additional insight into model behavior. Here, we introduce a process-aware inference framework in which local evidence sources interact through regulated negotiation, generating a measurable inference trajectory. We instantiated this framework in Raman spectroscopy by partitioning spectra into adjacent macro-bands that function as semi-autonomous agents contributing local class evidence. From the trajectories, we defined Decision Geometry (DG) as a descriptor of total reconciliation effort and effective Regulated Early Decision Geometry (eREDG) as a descriptor of early-stage negotiated dynamics. We evaluated the framework on a three-class melanoma Raman dataset, a small grouped in vivo diabetes Raman cohort, and a larger external 5-class bacteria/yeast Raman dataset comprising 10,000 training/validation spectra and 2500 independent external-test spectra. We showed that conventional classification accuracy cannot capture qualitative differences in inference trajectories, whereas DG reveals spectral conflict and regulatory strength. Under regulated regimes, eREDG further stratifies correct and incorrect predictions without access to ground truth. Finally, band-resolved H1 conflict analysis was localized to Raman regions. We propose this framework as a proof-of-principle, process-aware method to complement conventional machine-learning pipelines, demonstrated here in Raman spectroscopy as a domain where inference depends on spectral bands evidence.

title: A soft-sensability index for pre-modeling predictability assessment and a mechanism-constrained latent-variable model for grade-structured soft sensors
abstract: Data-driven soft sensors for grade-structured and campaign-structured chemical processes are conventionally validated by cross-validation, yet in these plants the procedure reports optimistic accuracy because grade identity is correlated with both the process features and the laboratory labels. A model that only reproduces the mean of each grade can then appear highly predictive. We develop a two-part chemometric methodology. The first part is the soft-sensability index, a pre-modeling statistic that separates the grade-corrected signal from a grade-confounding null. The null is generated by permuting labels within grade-by-campaign blocks, and both the time-ordered score and the null are estimated with time-ordered and moving-block resampling so that serial correlation does not distort the test. The second part is a mechanism-constrained latent-variable model that fixes a Mayo-Lewis copolymerization manifold as a physics anchor and fits a machine-learning residual on features deflated against that anchor. On an industrial styrene-acrylonitrile solution-polymerization soft sensor, naive validation rejects the no-signal null on every synthetic replicate, whereas the proposed test stays at its nominal level of 0.04. The index also shows that a color property with a low time-ordered coefficient of determination of 0.47 contributes the largest grade-corrected gain of any property, a reversal that conventional metrics obscure. The physics anchor recovers apparent reactivity ratios that absorb the steady-state offset between feed and reactor composition, and lowers unseen-grade extrapolation error from 2.3 to 0.9 wt% relative to a purely data-driven model. With four held-out grades this is not distinguishable from the physics anchor alone.

title: A preprocessing framework for calibration transfer of near-infrared spectroscopic data
abstract: Preprocessing is essential for near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopic data to eliminate unintended artifacts and enhance the performance of calibration models. However, preprocessing pipelines selected only by source-domain performance may transfer poorly when target-domain spectral data are affected by instrument-induced covariate shift. This study presents an unsupervised, threshold-free preprocessing-selection framework for NIR calibration transfer. The framework employs a genetic algorithm to efficiently generate candidate preprocessing workflows. Its key innovation lies in a dual-objective selection criterion: it jointly optimizes source-domain accuracy (root mean square error of cross-validation, RMSECV) and cross-domain prediction distribution alignment, quantified by the Wasserstein distance (WD) computed from unlabeled target-domain spectra. By normalizing both metrics and selecting the candidate with the minimal sum of squared normalized values, the framework eliminates the need for a subjective eligibility threshold, a critical limitation of existing MMD-based selection methods. Experiments on two real-world datasets evaluated the proposed framework against source-domain CV-based selection, unsupervised transfer baselines (domain-invariant partial least squares (PLS) variants and MMD-based preprocessing selection), and supervised target-predicting-target modeling. Results showed that the proposed framework reduced target-domain prediction errors compared to source-domain CV-based selection and domain-invariant PLS variants, while achieving competitive performance against the MMD-based selection baseline.

title: Multimodal fusion of skin lesion images and NIR spectroscopy: A novel dataset for classification evaluation
abstract: Early diagnosis of skin cancer is essential to improve treatment success rates, given its high incidence and clinical complexity. Although computer-aided diagnosis systems have advanced significantly, exclusive reliance on visual data may overlook relevant molecular information contained in spectral data. This work proposes a multimodal approach for the automated classification of skin lesions, integrating visual features extracted by different Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures, specifically FocalNet, DenseNet, RegNet, and ResNet50, with Near-Infrared (NIR) spectral data processed by Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). For this purpose, a new dataset called I+NIR-SC-UFES was introduced, composed of images collected using a smartphone and spectral samples collected using a portable MicroNIR spectrometer. The methodology investigates two spectral integration strategies: the use of latent vectors extracted by the VAE encoder and feature selection based on SHAP values, aiming to identify the spectral components with the greatest diagnostic impact. For modality fusion, an attention mechanism is employed, allowing the model to dynamically adjust the importance assigned to each type of information (visual and spectral) during the analysis process. Comparative experiments were conducted to evaluate the performance of the different architectures and the impact of SHAP-based explainability in relation to the pure latent space. The results indicate that combining advanced image analysis techniques with spectral data interpretation can lead to more accurate and interpretable diagnostic support systems, benefiting screening and disease detection.

title: RL-optimized CNN–BiLSTM: A multi-layer adaptive deep learning framework for heart disease diagnosis using IoT sensor data and reinforcement learning
abstract: Cardiovascular disease remains a leading cause of premature mortality worldwide, highlighting the need for accurate, continuous, and adaptive cardiac monitoring. This study proposes a three-layer IoT–Fog–Cloud framework integrated with a reinforcement learning (RL)-optimized CNN–BiLSTM model for early heart disease detection. The IoT layer continuously acquires physiological signals, including ECG, heart rate, and blood pressure; the fog layer performs preprocessing, feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, and classification; and the cloud layer supports long-term storage and large-scale analytics. The key novelty of this study is the joint integration of multimodal physiological and clinical data with dual RL-based optimization within the IoT–Fog–Cloud architecture. Specifically, a Deep Q-Network (DQN) adaptively selects discriminative features, while a policy-gradient mechanism dynamically optimizes classification decision thresholds, enabling the CNN–BiLSTM model to adapt beyond conventional static feature-selection and classification approaches. The framework was evaluated using the Cleveland, Hungarian, and Framingham cardiovascular datasets. Data preprocessing included normalization, anomaly detection, feature extraction, and PCA-based dimensionality reduction. The proposed RL-optimized CNN–BiLSTM achieved accuracies of 96.4%, 95.7%, and 94.1%, with AUC values of 0.98, 0.97, and 0.96, on the Cleveland, Hungarian, and Framingham datasets, respectively. Robustness testing under Gaussian noise further demonstrated stable predictive performance across heterogeneous datasets. These findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed adaptive framework for real-time cardiac risk assessment, remote patient monitoring, and intelligent clinical decision support.

title: Hierarchical conditional diffusion augmentation and sparse spectral fusion for NIR concentration prediction
abstract: Concentration prediction based on near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy is widely used in food inspection, environmental monitoring, and chemical analysis. However, high-dimensional redundancy, complex nonlinear responses, and limited sample sizes restrict prediction performance. To address these challenges, this study proposes a unified framework, termed HCD-VAE-SpecSparseFusion, integrating hierarchical conditional latent diffusion generation with sparse spectral feature modeling. A Hierarchical Conditional Diffusion Variational Autoencoder (HCD-VAE) generates high-fidelity augmented spectra through multi-scale latent representations and conditional diffusion. A dual-branch regression network, SpecSparseFusion, combines residual convolution and sparse attention to jointly capture local absorption features and global spectral dependencies. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed HCD-VAE effectively improves spectral augmentation quality and enhances model robustness under limited-sample conditions. Under the optimal experimental configuration, the proposed HCD-VAE-SpecSparseFusion framework achieved an R2 of 0.95, an RMSE of 0.003, and an RPD of 4.46 on the independent test set. Across ten independent runs with different random seeds, the framework achieved an average R2 of 0.89 ± 0.07 and an average RPD of 3.43 ± 1.15, demonstrating good robustness and reproducibility. However, the generalizability of the proposed framework to other water pollutants and diverse NIR spectrometers requires further investigation.

title: Two-dimensional NIR spectral representation of pharmaceuticals and wheat and intelligent quantitative analysis of constituents
abstract: Traditional one-dimensional near-infrared spectroscopy only reflects the variation of spectral intensity with wavelengths, and analytical models are difficult to mine the coupling correlation features among different wavelengths. Meanwhile, traditional linear machine learning and one-dimensional deep learning models suffer from insufficient nonlinear fitting ability, weak capability in extracting global wavelength-dependent information, and poor anti-interference performance and small-sample generalization ability, which greatly limits the high-precision non-destructive quantitative detection of pharmaceutical and agricultural products in near-infrared spectral analysis. To solve the above problems, this paper adopts six two-dimensional encoding strategies to convert one-dimensional spectra into two-dimensional feature matrices to characterize the implicit correlation information between wavelengths. Customized optimization of deep learning models is carried out according to the differentiated spectral characteristics of two application scenarios, and the Difference Index (DI) achieves superior performance in both cases: (1) In the application of tablet active ingredient detection with high signal-to-noise ratio and high-dimensional features, the DI-S-ViT model is constructed by combining two-dimensional spectral characterization built via DI with the spectral Vision Transformer architecture. It captures global wavelength dependencies through multi-head self-attention, achieving R2 = 0.9757 and RPD = 6.420 on the test set; (2) For the scenario of single wheat kernel protein detection characterized by strong scattering noise and limited sample size, the DI-S-ResNet18 model adopting optimal DI encoding and a modified residual network is used. The residual structure improves the robustness of the model with small samples, with R2 = 0.9321 and RPD = 3.873 on the test set. In addition, a lightweight S-CNN is established as the baseline model to objectively validate the performance advantages of the two customized models. Experimental results show that two-dimensional spectral encoding effectively compensates for the inability of one-dimensional spectra to characterize band coupling information. Compared with the optimal one-dimensional baseline models on the two datasets, the RMSEP decreased by 16.56% in the tablet scenario and 24.74% in the wheat scenario. The prediction accuracy and generalization ability of the new method are significantly improved. This method can provide a high-precision modeling approach for non-destructive quantitative detection of pharmaceutical tablets and grain agricultural products.

title: Multi-label feature selection via pseudo-label dependence and dual hypergraph regularization
abstract: Existing multi-label feature selection methods aim to learn latent shared structure from both instance and label spaces, projecting them into a unified representation to guide the feature selection process. Despite their effectiveness, these methods rely on a binary label space that is inconsistent with continuous real-world supervision, consider only instance-level correlations while neglecting label correlations, and employ generic graph regularization that fails to capture higher-order dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose a novel method named Multi-label Feature Selection via Pseudo-label Dependence and Dual Hypergraph Regularization (PLDHR). PLDHR replaces binary ground-truth label space with a continuous pseudo-label space, enabling the learned shared structure to better capture latent supervisory information. It further introduces dual-graph regularization to jointly model both instance and label correlations. Moreover, hypergraph-based regularization is incorporated to effectively capture higher-order dependencies. Extensive experiments conducted on 9 benchmark datasets and 4 large-scale benchmark datasets demonstrate that, compared with 16 state-of-the-art methods, PLDHR consistently achieves superior overall performance across six evaluation metrics, highlighting its effectiveness and robustness.

title: Causal memory-enhanced temporal structural root-cause analysis for industrial multivariate process anomalies
abstract: Fault propagation in industrial processes can amplify downstream deviations and obscure the observable source. Causal memory-enhanced temporal structural root-cause analysis (CM-TSRCA) is proposed to localize event sources by combining onset information, lagged predictive support, and source-responsibility evidence. Candidates are selected using deviation magnitude and relative onset, retaining weak initiators while preserving all observed channels for structural estimation. Window-conditioned support is regularized by nominal prototypes retrieved from causal memory. The memory contribution is adjusted according to operating context, local-memory disagreement, and retrieval ambiguity. Predictive inconsistency, downstream explanatory reach, temporal precedence, repair consistency, and upstream explainability are then combined to rank candidate sources. The method is evaluated on three controlled benchmarks, the causRCA hardware-in-the-loop fault dataset, and historical distributed control system records from two operational polyester esterification lines. On Lorenz96, CM-TSRCA achieves a directed-support F1 of 0.867±0.034 and top-1 localization accuracy (AC@1) of 0.900±0.030. On polyester Lines A and B, AC@1 reaches 0.465 and 0.399, and average cumulative accuracy over ranks 1–10 (Avg@10) reaches 0.815 and 0.822, respectively, against prespecified observable-source or source-proxy labels. On causRCA Hydraulics, CM-TSRCA achieves the highest Avg@10 among the compared methods at every evaluated sensor-noise and channel-loss level.

title: Non-destructive hyperspectral prediction of oxytetracycline concentration in oilseed rape leaves using an adaptive spectral patch attention network
abstract: Increasing antibiotic inputs into agricultural environments have increased the need for rapid residue screening in crop tissues. Conventional chromatographic methods provide reliable quantification but require complex, destructive sample preparation, which limits the rapid and non-destructive assessment of large numbers of leaf samples. Visible and near-infrared hyperspectral images were acquired from 1500 oilseed rape leaves exposed to ten oxytetracycline (OTC) treatment levels ranging from 0 to 200 mg L−1. Reference OTC concentrations determined by high-performance liquid chromatography for 1350 leaves were used as regression targets. Following spectral characterization, conventional machine learning and one-dimensional deep learning models were evaluated. An Adaptive Spectral Patch Attention Network (ASPA-Net) was developed to integrate global spectral variation, local spectral morphology, and inter-patch relationships for OTC prediction. Across 50 repeated random train–validation–test splits, ASPA-Net achieved a test R2 of 0.924 ± 0.011, an RMSE of 1.37 ± 0.10 mg kg−1, and an MAE of 1.03 ± 0.07 mg kg−1, and an RPD of 3.66 ± 0.26. Ablation experiments confirmed the complementary contributions of global spectral and local morphological features. Feature selection and internal attention analyses consistently identified the red and red-edge region (640-726 nm) as particularly informative, with additional contributions from the short-wavelength visible region (398-436 nm). These findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining visible and near-infrared hyperspectral imaging with ASPA-Net for rapid, non-destructive prediction of OTC concentrations in oilseed rape leaves under the evaluated conditions.

title: Outliers by design: a PCA-based framework for controlled multivariate outlier generation
abstract: Synthetic outliers test multivariate methods, but the usual devices (shifting a value, scaling a row, adding noise) specify how an observation is perturbed, not what it becomes: how atypical the result is, and in what sense, is left to the data. Principal Component Analysis answers both questions with two statistics: Hotelling's T2, for departure within the model, and the Squared Prediction Error, for departure from it. We present DOC (Designed Outlier Construction), which builds such an observation by displacing a seed observation in two components, one per statistic, attaining prescribed values of both exactly and independently. DOC also controls that displacement. Linear requirements can be imposed on either component or jointly on both, leaving a variable, a sum or a ratio untouched, and where the residual displacement goes is a further choice that neither statistic reveals. What the requirements cost is the number of directions they actually remove, known in advance, so an unattainable specification is refused, not approximated. What the requirements leave undetermined is not one observation but a set of them, all meeting the specification exactly and differing in the original variables. A selector vector picks one, and it is the only element of the construction that may be drawn at random; the rest is deterministic and in closed form. A specification met exactly may still be implausible, and the set can be searched on domain grounds. Five datasets, from four variables to seven hundred, measure what each choice costs.
